Fine-Tuning Small Multimodal Models

11 papers on how small open models read text, see images and hear speech, and how to fine-tune them with LoRA and QLoRA on a single free GPU.

Introduction

Before the papers: a visual primer

11 papers · about 20 minutes to read

In a typical fine-tuning project you take a small open model, teach it a task that uses text, images and voice, and measure what changed. The eleven papers describe the models you can start from and the method that makes it affordable. This tab explains the ideas they take for granted: tokens, transformers, how a model sees and hears, LoRA and QLoRA on a free GPU, and how to measure results fairly. It ends with a map of the papers.

Reading guide

This tab answers one question: what do you need to know before the eleven papers make sense? The answer is a short visual primer for anyone starting a fine-tuning project. It starts with a whole project in one picture, then explains tokens, transformers, how a model sees images and hears speech, and what omni models are. Next come LoRA and QLoRA on a free sixteen gigabyte T4, and then data, metrics, normalization and fairness for your experiments. It closes with a map of all eleven papers and a glossary. After this tab come QLoRA, the fine-tuning tool, then the vision language models TinyLLaVA Factory and SmolVLM, the speech models Voxtral and Voxtral Realtime, the efficient backbone LFM2, and the omni models MiniMind-O, Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni, MiniCPM-o 4.5 and Gemma 4. Every block has a Guide note like this one.

§1A fine-tuning project in one picture

Three kinds of input go in, a text answer comes out. If your model cannot hear, a speech-to-text model does the listening for it.

§2From text to tokens

A model never reads letters. Text is cut into tokens, each token becomes a number, and each number becomes a vector.

§3Transformers and language models in 5 minutes

Every model in the atlas has a transformer language model at its centre (LFM2 mixes in short convolutions). Two ideas matter for you: attention mixes information between tokens, and memory grows with parameters and with sequence length.

(1)\[ \operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V \]

Scores = queries times keys, scaled by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) and turned into weights by softmax; the output is the weighted mix of values. The score matrix is tokens × tokens, so cost grows with the square of sequence length.

Guide

This is the attention formula. Q holds the queries, K the keys and V the values. Multiplying Q by K transposed scores every pair of tokens, dividing by the square root of d k keeps the scores in a stable range, and softmax turns each row into weights that sum to one. The output mixes the values with those weights. The score matrix is tokens by tokens, so cost grows with the square of the sequence length.

(2)\[ \text{weight memory} \approx \text{parameters} \times \text{bytes per parameter} \]

A 2B model in FP16 (2 bytes) needs about 4 GB just for weights; in 4-bit (0.5 byte) about 1 GB, plus small scale constants.

Guide

Weight memory is roughly the number of parameters times the bytes used for each one. A two billion parameter model at two bytes per parameter, which is FP16, needs about four gigabytes, and in four bits, half a byte each, about one gigabyte plus a little for scale constants. This one line explains why QLoRA stores the frozen model in four bits, and it is the first check before you pick a model for the free T4.

Weights only, 1 GB = 10⁹ bytes. Training adds gradients, optimizer states and activations on top.
PrecisionBytes / parameter2B model7B modelWhere you meet it
FP3248 GB28 GBoptimizer states, master weights
FP16 / BF1624 GB14 GBnormal inference; T4: FP16 only

4-bit (NF4)0.5≈ 1 GB≈ 3.5 GBQLoRA frozen base
Guide

The table applies the memory rule to a two billion and a seven billion parameter model at four precisions. Read across a row: each halving of the bytes halves the memory, from twenty eight gigabytes for a seven billion model in FP32 down to about three and a half in four-bit NF4. These are weights only. Training adds gradients, optimizer states and activations, and remember that the T4 runs FP16 but not fast BF16.

§4How a model sees

An image is cut into small square patches, a vision encoder turns them into features, and a projector translates the features into "visual tokens" that sit next to the text tokens.

§5How a model hears and speaks

Sound is turned into a picture-like spectrogram, an audio encoder turns that into frames, and an adapter packs frames into audio tokens for the LLM. Speaking back runs the chain in reverse with codec tokens.

§6Omni models

An omni model puts all encoders in front of one language model, the Thinker, and adds a Talker that speaks. Four papers here, plus one larger reference model, are omni models.

§7Fine-tuning without a big GPU

Full fine-tuning updates every weight and needs memory for gradients and optimizer states of all of them. LoRA freezes the model and trains two thin matrices per layer; QLoRA also stores the frozen model in 4 bits.

(3)\[ W' = W + \frac{\alpha}{r}\,BA,\qquad B\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r},\; A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times k},\; r \ll \min(d,k) \]

LoRA: the frozen weight \(W\) plus a trainable low-rank update. \(r\) is the rank, \(\alpha\) a scaling constant (QLoRA's recipe: \(r=64,\ \alpha=16\)). Trainable numbers per matrix: \(r(d+k)\) instead of \(dk\).

Guide

This is the LoRA update. The new weight W prime equals the frozen weight W plus B times A, scaled by alpha over r. B has d rows and r columns, A has r rows and k columns, and the rank r is much smaller than both sides, so only r times d plus k numbers are trained. QLoRA's recipe uses rank sixty four and alpha sixteen, and found that adapters on every linear layer matter more than the rank.

§8Data, metrics and experiments

Evaluation is about measuring honestly: the same test set, the same metric and the same text normalization for every model you compare.

(4)\[ \text{WER}=\frac{S+D+I}{N} \]

Word error rate: substitutions \(S\), deletions \(D\) and insertions \(I\) needed to turn the model's transcript into the reference, divided by the number of reference words \(N\). Lower is better; it can exceed 100%. CER is the same on characters.

Guide

Word error rate counts the edits needed to turn the model's transcript into the reference. S is substitutions, D is deletions and I is insertions, and their sum is divided by N, the number of words in the reference. Lower is better, and because insertions have no limit it can go above one hundred percent. Character error rate is the same idea on characters. The next figure works through one example by hand.

(5)\[ F_1=\frac{2PR}{P+R},\qquad P=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\quad R=\frac{TP}{TP+FN} \]

F1 is the harmonic mean of precision \(P\) and recall \(R\) (true/false positives and negatives). For short text answers it is often computed on overlapping words; exact match (EM) counts only identical answers.

Guide

F one combines precision and recall into one number. Precision P is the share of your predicted items that are correct, true positives over true plus false positives. Recall R is the share of correct items you found, true positives over true positives plus false negatives. F one is two P R over P plus R, their harmonic mean. For short text answers it is often computed on overlapping words, while exact match only credits identical answers.

§10Glossary

Glossary

Adapter
A small trainable module added to a frozen model; in LoRA, the matrices A and B.
ASR (speech-to-text)
Automatic speech recognition: turns spoken audio into a written transcript.
Attention
The layer where each token weighs and mixes information from all other tokens.
BF16 / FP16
16-bit number formats (2 bytes); the free T4 supports FP16 but not fast BF16.
CER
Character error rate: WER computed on characters instead of words.
Chat template
The model-specific format with special tokens that marks system, user and assistant turns.
Codec tokens
Discrete codes for short slices of sound that a codec decoder turns back into a waveform.
Context length
The maximum number of tokens the model can read at once.
Embedding
The vector of numbers that represents one token inside the model.
Exact match (EM)
Share of answers identical to the reference, usually after normalization.
F1
Harmonic mean of precision and recall; for text answers, often on overlapping words.
Fairness gap
The difference in a metric between two groups, such as male and female speakers.
Fine-tuning
Further training of a pre-trained model on a small task-specific dataset.
Gradient checkpointing
Recomputing activations during the backward pass to save memory at some cost in time.
Instruction-tuned
A model further trained to follow requests in a chat format ("Instruct", "IT").
Licence
The legal terms for using a model or dataset, for example Apache 2.0 or CC BY.
LLM
Large language model: a transformer trained to predict the next token.
Log-mel spectrogram
A picture of sound: energy per frequency band over time, on a hearing-like scale.
LoRA
Low-rank adaptation: freeze W and train a thin update B·A beside it.
Model card
A short document stating a model's intended use, data, results and limitations.
NF4
4-bit NormalFloat, the QLoRA data type whose 16 levels suit bell-shaped weights.
Normalization (text)
Putting text in one standard form: case, punctuation, diacritics, numbers.
Omni model
One model that accepts text, images, audio (often video) and may answer in speech.
Parameters
The learned numbers in a model's weight matrices; "2B" means about two billion.
Patch
A small square of pixels (for example 16 × 16) that a vision transformer treats as one token.
Pixel shuffle
Folding r × r neighbouring visual features into one token to cut the count by r².
Projector
A small network (often an MLP) that maps encoder features into the LLM's embedding space.
QLoRA
LoRA on top of a base model stored in 4 bits, so fine-tuning fits one GPU.
Quantization
Storing numbers with fewer bits (8 or 4 instead of 16) to save memory.
Rank (r)
The inner width of the LoRA matrices; larger r means more trainable parameters.
SigLIP / CLIP
Vision encoders pre-trained to match images with their captions.
Streaming
Producing output while the input is still arriving, with a small fixed delay.
T4
The NVIDIA GPU with 16 GB of memory on free Colab and Kaggle.
Talker
The part of an omni model that turns the Thinker's hidden states into speech.
Thinker
The main language model of an omni model: reads all inputs, writes text.
Token
The unit a model reads and writes: a word piece, or a slice of an image or sound.
ViT
Vision Transformer: a transformer that reads an image as a sequence of patches.
VLM
Vision-language model: reads images and text, writes text.
WER
Word error rate: (substitutions + deletions + insertions) divided by reference words.
Whisper
A widely used open speech-to-text model whose encoder several atlas models reuse.
Guide

The glossary collects forty terms used across the atlas, in alphabetical order, each with a one-line plain definition. Use it as a lookup table while you read the papers, and as a checklist for yourself: if you can explain tokens, encoders, projectors, LoRA, QLoRA, word error rate and normalization in your own words, you are ready. Several terms, such as Thinker, Talker and codec tokens, only appear in the omni papers.

The fine-tuning toolkit

QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs

Tim Dettmers*, Artidoro Pagnoni*, Ari Holtzman, Luke Zettlemoyer · University of Washington · arXiv 2305.14314, May 2023 (NeurIPS 2023)

QLoRA freezes a pretrained language model, stores its weights in a new 4-bit data type (NormalFloat, NF4), and trains only small low-rank adapters (LoRA) whose gradients flow back through the 4-bit weights. With double quantization and paged optimizers, a 65B model can be finetuned on one 48 GB GPU, and the 4-bit adapters match 16-bit full finetuning on the benchmarks tested. This is the method behind most low-cost fine-tuning projects today.

Base weights
4-bit NF4, frozen
Trained
LoRA on all linear layers
65B finetune memory
> 780 GB → < 48 GB
Const. overhead (DQ)
0.5 → 0.127 bit/param
Guanaco 65B, Vicuna bench.
99.3% of ChatGPT
Models trained
> 1,000 (80M–65B)
Reading guide

QLoRA asks whether you can finetune a large language model on a single GPU without losing the quality of full sixteen bit finetuning. Its answer is yes: freeze the model, store its weights in a new four bit data type called NormalFloat, and train only small low-rank adapters on every linear layer. The tab starts with the big picture, then the memory problem, the method in four steps, every equation, the six figures redrawn, the result tables, and finally a box that turns the paper into practical advice. QLoRA opens the atlas of eleven papers because it is the fine-tuning tool the other papers build on in practice. After it come the vision language models TinyLLaVA Factory and SmolVLM, the speech models Voxtral and Voxtral Realtime, LFM2, and the omni models MiniMind-O, Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni, MiniCPM-o 4.5 and Gemma 4.

§0Before you read

To follow this paper you only need three ideas: how many bytes a model's weights take, what it means to round weights to 4 bits, and how LoRA trains a tiny add-on instead of the whole model. QLoRA combines them so that a large model can be fine-tuned on one GPU, and it is the recipe that lets you fine-tune a small model on a free Colab or Kaggle GPU.

Terms used in this paper

Parameter (weight)
One learned number inside the model. "7B" means about seven billion of them; each costs memory according to how many bits store it.
Fine-tuning
Continuing to train a pretrained model on your own, smaller dataset so it gets better at your task.
LoRA
Low-Rank Adaptation: freeze the original weights and train two small matrices per layer whose product is added to the frozen weight.
Rank \(r\)
The inner width of the two LoRA matrices. Small ranks such as 8 to 64 mean very few trained parameters; the paper finds rank matters little.
Quantization
Storing numbers with fewer bits by rounding them to a small set of allowed levels, plus a scale to map them back.
NF4 (NormalFloat 4-bit)
The paper's new 4-bit data type: 16 levels placed to suit bell-shaped (normally distributed) weights, with an exact zero.
Double quantization
Quantizing the per-block scale constants too, which cuts their cost from about 0.5 to about 0.127 bits per weight.
Paged optimizers
Optimizer states kept in NVIDIA unified memory, so they can move to CPU RAM during a memory spike instead of crashing training.
BF16 (bfloat16)
A 16-bit number format used for computing. QLoRA stores weights in 4 bits but turns them back into BF16 for each multiplication. The Colab T4 does not support BF16 efficiently, so you will use FP16 there.
Optimizer states (Adam)
Extra numbers the Adam optimizer keeps for every trained parameter (two running averages). For full fine-tuning they cost more memory than the weights.
Gradient checkpointing
Saving memory by not storing all intermediate activations and recomputing them in the backward pass, at the cost of extra compute time.
MMLU
Massive Multitask Language Understanding: multiple-choice questions over 57 subjects, scored by accuracy. The paper uses it to check that 4-bit training loses nothing.
Vicuna benchmark and Elo
A set of 80 chatbot prompts. Answers are compared in pairs by GPT-4 or humans, and Elo ratings, as in chess, turn wins into a ranking.
Guanaco
The paper's chatbot family: LLaMA models fine-tuned with QLoRA on the OASST1 dataset. The 65B version was trained on one 48 GB GPU.
Guide

These fourteen terms are the vocabulary the paper takes for granted. The core ones are LoRA and its rank, quantization and the NF4 data type, double quantization and paged optimizers. BF16 is the sixteen bit format used for computing, though on a Colab T4 you will use FP16. MMLU, the Vicuna benchmark, Elo ratings and Guanaco appear in the results. Come back here whenever a term in the tab stops you.

§1Big picture

QLoRA changes how you store the frozen model (4-bit NF4 plus double-quantized constants) and what you train (LoRA on every linear layer). Compute still happens in 16-bit, so accuracy matches 16-bit finetuning while memory drops about 16 times.

§2The problem

  • Existing 4-bit methods (GPTQ, LLM.int8) are for inference; they break down when you train through them.
  • Plain FP4 / Int4 grids waste levels, because trained weights are roughly normally distributed, not uniform.
  • Small blocks help precision but cost 0.5 extra bits per weight in FP32 constants.
  • Long sequences with gradient checkpointing cause memory spikes that crash single-GPU runs.
  • The usual LoRA recipe (adapters on query and value only) does not match full finetuning on large models (Fig. 2).

§3Method

  1. Build NF4. Take quantiles of a standard normal so each of the 16 levels covers an equal share of weights (Eq. 4), make the grid asymmetric so zero is exact, and normalize it to [−1, 1].
  2. Quantize the frozen weights once. Split every weight matrix into blocks of 64, scale each block by its absmax constant c₂, round to the nearest NF4 level.
  3. Double-quantize the constants. Group 256 constants c₂, subtract their mean, store them in FP8 with one FP32 constant c₁ (0.5 → 0.127 bit per parameter).
  4. Attach LoRA everywhere. Add a BF16 adapter s·X·L₁L₂ to every linear layer of the transformer (Eq. 3, 5).
  5. Train. Forward and backward dequantize W to BF16 on the fly (Eq. 6); gradients flow through W, but only L₁, L₂ get weight gradients and Adam states.
  6. Page the optimizer. Adam states live in NVIDIA unified memory and move to CPU RAM only when a long batch would overflow the GPU.
Guide

The procedure has a one-time part and a training part. Once, you build the NF4 grid, quantize every frozen weight in blocks of sixty four, and compress the block constants again with double quantization. Then you attach LoRA to every linear layer and train: weights are dequantized to sixteen bits on the fly, only adapters get gradients, and optimizer states page to CPU memory if a long batch would overflow the GPU.

Recipe used for all Guanaco runs (Appendix B.2), written as a Hugging Face config (our transcription of the paper's settings, not code from the paper) bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4", # NF4 storage type bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True, # DQ bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16) # fp16 on a T4 lora = LoraConfig(r=64, lora_alpha=16, lora_dropout=0.1, # 0.05 for 33B/65B target_modules="all-linear", # LoRA on every linear layer task_type="CAUSAL_LM") args = TrainingArguments(optim="paged_adamw_32bit", # paged optimizer learning_rate=2e-4, # 1e-4 for 33B/65B lr_scheduler_type="constant", max_grad_norm=0.3, adam_beta2=0.999, group_by_length=True, gradient_checkpointing=True, per_device_train_batch_size=16) loss on the response tokens only (Table 10)
Guide

This block turns the paper's Appendix B settings into the Hugging Face configuration you will actually type. The quantization config asks for NF4 with double quantization, the LoRA config puts rank sixty four adapters with alpha sixteen on all linear layers, and the training arguments pick the paged AdamW optimizer, a constant learning rate of two times ten to the minus four, and gradient clipping at 0.3. On a T4, switch the compute type to float sixteen.

§4Every equation

(1)\[ \mathbf{X}^{\text{Int8}} = \operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac{127}{\operatorname{absmax}(\mathbf{X}^{\text{FP32}})}\,\mathbf{X}^{\text{FP32}}\right) = \operatorname{round}\!\left(c^{\text{FP32}}\cdot \mathbf{X}^{\text{FP32}}\right) \]

Absmax quantization: scale the tensor so its largest magnitude maps to 127, then round. \(c\) is the quantization constant (scale).

Guide

Equation one is ordinary absmax quantization to eight bit integers. X FP32 is the full precision tensor; it is multiplied by 127 divided by its largest absolute value, and rounded. That factor is the quantization constant c. Because the largest value sets the scale, outliers waste the grid, which motivates blockwise quantization and, later, NF4.

(2)\[ \operatorname{dequant}\!\left(c^{\text{FP32}}, \mathbf{X}^{\text{Int8}}\right) = \frac{\mathbf{X}^{\text{Int8}}}{c^{\text{FP32}}} = \mathbf{X}^{\text{FP32}} \]

Dequantization divides by the same constant (equality up to rounding error).

Guide

Equation two undoes equation one: divide the stored integers by the same constant c to get back the full precision values, up to rounding error. QLoRA performs this dequantization every time a frozen weight is used, and equation six applies it twice.

\[ \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{b\times h}\ \to\ n = \frac{b\times h}{B}\ \text{blocks},\ \text{each with its own } c_i \]

Blockwise quantization: flatten the tensor, cut it into n blocks of size B, apply Eq. 1 to each block.

Guide

The input tensor X, with b rows and h columns, is flattened and cut into n blocks of size B, so n equals b times h divided by B. Each block gets its own constant c i. Smaller blocks limit the damage of an outlier but create more constants to store.

(3)\[ \mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W} + s\,\mathbf{X}\mathbf{L}_1\mathbf{L}_2,\qquad \mathbf{L}_1\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times r},\ \mathbf{L}_2\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times o} \]

LoRA: the frozen projection W plus a trainable rank-r product L₁L₂ scaled by s (in practice s = α / r).

Guide

Equation three is LoRA. Y equals X times the frozen weight W, plus s times X times L one times L two. L one has h rows and r columns, L two has r rows and o columns, and r, the rank, is small, so the correction has few parameters. The scalar s scales the update. Only L one and L two are trained.

(4)\[ q_i = \frac{1}{2}\left(Q_X\!\left(\frac{i}{2^k+1}\right) + Q_X\!\left(\frac{i+1}{2^k+1}\right)\right) \]

NF-k levels: \(Q_X\) is the quantile function of \(N(0,1)\); each level is the midpoint of two neighbouring quantiles, so every bin holds an equal share of normal data.

Guide

Equation four builds the NF4 levels. Q X is the quantile function of the standard normal distribution. Each level q i is the average of two neighbouring quantiles, so every bin catches the same expected number of normally distributed weights. With k equal to four this gives sixteen levels before normalizing them to the range minus one to one.

\[ \text{NF}k = \operatorname{norm}_{[-1,1]}\Big(\{q_i\}_{2^{k-1}\ \text{negative}} \cup \{q_i\}_{2^{k-1}+1\ \text{positive}}\Big)\ \text{with the duplicate } 0 \text{ removed} \ \Rightarrow\ 2^k \text{ values} \]

Asymmetric construction that keeps an exact zero; for k = 4 this gives the 16 values of Appendix E.

Guide

A symmetric grid from equation four has no exact zero, yet zero matters for padding and zero weights. So QLoRA takes eight levels for the negative side and nine for the positive side, merges them, and drops the duplicated zero. The result is exactly sixteen values, the NF4 table in Appendix E.

\[ \frac{32}{64} = 0.5\ \text{bit}\quad\longrightarrow\quad \frac{8}{64} + \frac{32}{64\cdot 256} = 0.127\ \text{bit}\qquad(\text{saving } 0.373\ \text{bit per parameter}) \]

Memory cost of the quantization constants before and after double quantization (block 64 for W, block 256 for c₂).

Guide

This line counts the cost of the quantization constants. Thirty two bits for every sixty four weights is half a bit per parameter. After double quantization it is eight over sixty four plus thirty two over sixty four times 256, which is 0.127 bits, a saving of 0.373 bits per parameter.

(5)\[ \mathbf{Y}^{\text{BF16}} = \mathbf{X}^{\text{BF16}}\,\operatorname{doubleDequant}\!\left(c_1^{\text{FP32}}, c_2^{k\text{-bit}}, \mathbf{W}^{\text{NF4}}\right) + \mathbf{X}^{\text{BF16}}\mathbf{L}_1^{\text{BF16}}\mathbf{L}_2^{\text{BF16}} \]

QLoRA for one linear layer: the frozen 4-bit path plus the 16-bit adapter path.

Guide

Equation five is QLoRA for one linear layer. The sixteen bit input X is multiplied by the double dequantized frozen weight, recovered from the NF4 weights and the two levels of constants c one and c two, and the adapter path X times L one times L two is added. It is exactly the zoom panel in the big picture.

(6)\[ \operatorname{doubleDequant}\!\left(c_1^{\text{FP32}}, c_2^{k\text{-bit}}, \mathbf{W}^{k\text{-bit}}\right) = \operatorname{dequant}\!\left(\operatorname{dequant}\!\left(c_1^{\text{FP32}}, c_2^{k\text{-bit}}\right), \mathbf{W}^{\text{4bit}}\right) = \mathbf{W}^{\text{BF16}} \]

First recover the block constants c₂ from FP8 using c₁, then use them to recover the BF16 weights. NF4 for W, FP8 for c₂.

Guide

Equation six defines double dequantization. First the eight bit block constants c two are recovered using the thirty two bit constant c one. Then those constants dequantize the four bit weights into a sixteen bit weight matrix. Weights use NF4 with blocks of sixty four, constants use FP8 with blocks of 256.

\[ \text{needed: } \frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{L}_i}\quad\text{not needed: } \frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{W}}\qquad \frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{L}_i}\ \text{uses}\ \frac{\partial \mathbf{X}}{\partial \mathbf{W}}\ \text{computed in BF16 via Eq. 5} \]

Only adapter gradients update parameters; the frozen weights are still used (dequantized) to pass gradients backwards.

Guide

Training needs the gradient of the error E with respect to the adapter matrices L i, but not with respect to the frozen weights W. Computing the adapter gradient still requires passing gradients back through W, done in sixteen bit after dequantizing. This is why no optimizer state is needed for the base model.

\[ E_A = \frac{1}{1+10^{(R_B-R_A)/400}},\qquad R_A \leftarrow R_A + K\,(S_A - E_A),\ \ K = 32,\ R_0 = 1000 \]

Standard Elo formula behind Tables 1 and 7 (the paper states K = 32, start 1,000 and the example 1100 vs 1000 ≈ 65% win rate, but does not print the formula).

Guide

This is the standard Elo formula behind the chatbot tournaments in Tables one and seven. E A is the expected win chance of model A given ratings R A and R B; after each match the rating moves by K times the surprise. The paper uses K of thirty two and a start of one thousand but does not print the formula itself.

\[ \text{cell}(x,y) = \frac{\#\,[x \text{ better than } y] - \#\,[y \text{ better than } x]}{\text{total number of judgments}} \]

Aggregated pairwise GPT-4 judgment used in Table 12 (range −1 to 1).

Guide

Each cell of Table twelve compares two systems: the number of times GPT-4 judged row x better than column y, minus the times it judged y better, divided by the total number of judgments. A value near one means x almost always wins, near zero means a tie.

Table thirteen is the complete ranking implied by the pairwise GPT-4 judgments: Guanaco sixty five and thirty three billion first, then Vicuna, ChatGPT, Bard, and the smaller Guanacos. Model sizes are listed to show that the four bit thirty three billion Guanaco at 21 gigabytes outranks the sixteen bit Vicuna at 26.

  • Precision: 4-bit NF4 QLoRA matches 16-bit LoRA and 16-bit full finetuning on GLUE, Super-NaturalInstructions (up to 3B) and MMLU (7B–65B). FP4 is about 1 point behind.
  • Data: a 9k-example high-quality dataset (OASST1) beats a 450k subsample of FLAN v2 on chatbot quality; MMLU and Vicuna scores do not agree on which dataset is best.
  • Evaluation caveats: GPT-4 favours the answer shown first and rates its own outputs higher (Elo 1348 vs 1176 from humans); system-level agreement with humans is moderate (Kendall τ = 0.43, Spearman r = 0.55), example-level weak (Fleiss κ = 0.25).
  • Limits: no full-finetuning comparison at 33B/65B, no 3-bit bases, and only a CrowS bias check.

§7Putting it into practice

  • Inputs: QLoRA is a finetuning method, not a model, and every model in the paper is text-only. To cover image and voice, apply QLoRA to one of the multimodal models in the next tabs, or to a text/vision model plus a separate speech-to-text model in a pipeline (transcribe the voice, then feed the text).
  • Fits a free T4? The paper's own numbers (Fig. 6) give about 6.9 GB for LLaMA-7B at batch 1 and 512 tokens with gradient checkpointing, so a model of 7B or less plausibly fits 16 GB. But image and audio tokens make sequences much longer and activation memory grows with them, so check with a real batch. The T4 has no native BF16 support: set the compute dtype to float16.
  • Where to put LoRA in a multimodal model: the paper's key finding is LoRA on all linear layers of the language model (Fig. 2); rank barely matters (Fig. 4). Quantize and adapt the LLM backbone. Keep the vision and audio encoders frozen (commonly left unquantized in 16-bit, as they are small). The projector is small: train it fully or give it LoRA. The paper does not test multimodal models, so treat these choices as an experiment and report them. Note that target_modules="all-linear" will also hit encoder layers, so list the LLM modules explicitly if you want only the backbone.
  • Recipe for a text + image + voice task: start from Appendix B.2 (r = 64, α = 16, LR 2e-4 constant, dropout 0.1, max grad norm 0.3, paged AdamW) and compute the loss on answer tokens only (Table 10). Quality beats quantity (Table 11), which suits a few hundred clean examples. Group-by-length gives an oscillating loss curve; say so when you report it.
  • Fairness and normalization: finetuning changed bias scores a lot (CrowS, Table 8), so measure your group gap (e.g. male vs female speakers, Arabic vs English) for both base and finetuned models. If you use an LLM as a judge, average both answer orders, as the paper found a strong order bias. The paper does not study text normalization; keep whatever normalization you choose identical for training and test data.
Guide

Use this box as your checklist before training. First decide how your pipeline covers text, image and voice, since QLoRA itself only fine-tunes a text model. Then check memory on a real batch, set float sixteen compute on the T4, put LoRA on the language model's linear layers, start from the paper's hyperparameters, and measure the group gap for both base and finetuned models.

Seeing: vision-language models

TinyLLaVA Factory: A Modularized Codebase for Small-scale Large Multimodal Models

Junlong Jia, Ying Hu, Xi Weng, Yiming Shi, Miao Li, Xingjian Zhang, Baichuan Zhou, Ziyu Liu, Jie Luo, Lei Huang, Ji Wu · Beihang University / Tsinghua University · arXiv 2405.11788, May 2024 · github.com/TinyLLaVA/TinyLLaVA_Factory

A small vision-language model is three parts: a vision tower that turns an image into features, a connector that maps those features into the language model's token space, and a small LLM that reads visual and text tokens together and writes the answer. TinyLLaVA Factory is an open PyTorch / Hugging Face codebase in which each of these parts, plus the chat template and the training recipe (frozen, full, LoRA or QLoRA per part), is a swappable "factory" chosen in a config file. It reproduces the TinyLLaVA models slightly better than the original code.

Inputs
Text + one image
LLMs
0.45B to 2.7B (6 families)
Vision towers
CLIP · SigLIP · DINOv2 · MoF
Recipes
frozen · full · LoRA · QLoRA
Best variant
Phi-2 + SigLIP: MME 1466.4
Test coverage
≈ 92% of code lines
Reading guide

TinyLLaVA Factory asks a practical question: how can a small team build, train and compare small vision-language models without rewriting code for every change? Its answer is a modular codebase in which the vision tower, the connector, the small language model, the chat template and the training recipe are each a swappable factory picked in a config file. It is software rather than a new model, and it reproduces the TinyLLaVA models slightly better than the original code. The tab moves from the big picture and the problem, through the method, a few background equations, the one figure, and the results, to a box of practical advice. Among the eleven papers it comes second, right after QLoRA, and opens the group on seeing, followed by SmolVLM. For anyone new to the field, it is the clearest picture of how an image becomes tokens a language model can read.

§0Before you read

This paper is about a codebase, not a new model, so you mainly need three ideas: how a photo becomes "visual tokens" a language model can read, what it means to freeze, fully train or LoRA-tune a part, and how a config file picks parts from a menu. It is in the atlas because it shows the simplest recipe for a small vision-language model (text + one image in, text out) and already ships LoRA and QLoRA training recipes; voice you add yourself.

Terms used in this paper

LMM / vision-language model
A "large multimodal model": a language model that also takes non-text input, here one image, and answers in text. TinyLLaVA models are small LMMs.
LLaVA
An earlier, widely copied open model and codebase ("Visual Instruction Tuning") that connects a CLIP vision encoder to an LLM. Its data format is the one this codebase expects.
Vision tower (ViT)
The image encoder: a Vision Transformer that splits an image into patches and outputs one feature vector per patch.
CLIP and SigLIP
Two vision encoders pre-trained to match images with captions, from OpenAI and Google. SigLIP uses a sigmoid loss instead of CLIP's softmax loss and scores higher in this paper.
Connector (projector)
The small network between vision tower and LLM. In the experiments it is a two-layer MLP with a GELU activation that maps image features to the LLM's embedding size.
Chat template
The fixed text format each LLM family expects (system message, user turn, assistant turn). It also decides which tokens are the answer the model is trained on.
Pre-training vs. supervised fine-tuning
Stage 1 aligns images with words, mostly on image-caption data; stage 2 (SFT) teaches the model to follow instructions on image-question-answer conversations.
Base and share recipes
The two training setups reproduced. "Base" trains only the connector in stage 1 on LLaVA-1.5 data; "share" also trains the LLM in stage 1 and uses ShareGPT4V data.
Factory pattern
A software design where objects are built from a name via a registry, so parts can be swapped in a config file without editing model code.
VQAv2, GQA, TextVQA
Visual question answering benchmarks, scored as accuracy: everyday photos, compositional reasoning about objects, and questions that require reading text in the image.
ScienceQA-IMG (SQA-I)
Multiple-choice school science questions that come with an image; the score is accuracy.
POPE
A benchmark that asks yes/no questions about whether an object is in the image, measuring object hallucination.
MME, MM-Vet, MMMU
Broader multimodal benchmarks. MME sums perception scores (so numbers are in the thousands), MM-Vet grades open answers with a GPT-4 judge, and MMMU has college-level multi-subject questions.
DeepSpeed ZeRO
A library feature that splits optimizer states, gradients and weights across GPUs to save memory in multi-GPU training. The codebase uses it through the Hugging Face trainer.
Guide

Keep this glossary open while you read. The key terms are vision tower, the image encoder; connector, the small network that turns image features into tokens; and chat template, the text format that decides which tokens are the training target. The benchmark names, such as TextVQA, POPE and MME, appear in the results table, and knowing what each one tests will help you choose your own metric.

§2Big picture

The paper contributes software, not a new model: the TinyLLaVA architecture made modular, with standard data, training and evaluation pipelines.

Anything you plug in (a new LLM, vision tower, connector or recipe) inherits a base class and is selected by name.

§3The problem

  • Training an LMM needs many pieces to agree: data preprocessing, chat template, model architecture and multi-stage recipe. Mistakes are easy.
  • Scaling LMMs up makes training unaffordable outside well-funded labs; small LLMs (0.45B to 2.7B) keep it within reach.
  • Existing codebases (LLaVA) were not designed for swapping components; Prismatic-VLMs is modular but does not use the factory pattern or ship this suite of parts.

§4Method

4.1 One pattern everywhere: factory + base class

4.2 Text path: the chat template

4.3 Training recipes: who is frozen, tuned or LoRA-tuned

  1. Data. Put image–conversation pairs in LLaVA format; images are resized / padded / normalised, text goes through the chat template of the chosen LLM.
  2. Model. Name an LLM, a vision tower and a connector in the config; three factories build them from their base classes.
  3. Recipe. Choose a training recipe that sets each component to frozen, full, partial, LoRA or QLoRA, and the matching save / load logic.
  4. Trainer. A Hugging Face Trainer runs training with gradient accumulation, DeepSpeed ZeRO and TensorBoard / Wandb logging.
  5. Two stages. Pre-train (feature alignment, mainly the connector), then supervised fine-tuning on instruction data.
  6. Evaluator. Score the model on 8 benchmarks (VQAv2, GQA, ScienceQA-IMG, TextVQA, MM-Vet, POPE, MME, MMMU).
Guide

These six steps are the life of one training run in the codebase. Data in LLaVA format goes through image preprocessing and the chat template, three factories build the model, a recipe decides what is trainable, and a Hugging Face trainer does the optimisation. Training runs in two stages, alignment then instruction tuning, and the evaluator scores eight benchmarks. Your own notebook can follow the same order, with a speech-to-text step added before the data stage.

§5Every equation

The paper contains no numbered or displayed equations. The three lines below are background, not from the paper: they write down what the codebase computes (the connector of Appendix A, the answer-only loss implied by "making labels", and the LoRA / QLoRA recipe it cites), so you can describe the model precisely in your own write-up.

(B1)\[ \mathbf{H}_v = g_\phi\big(f_{\text{VT}}(\mathbf{X}_v)\big), \qquad g_\phi(\mathbf{z}) = \mathbf{W}_2\,\operatorname{GELU}(\mathbf{W}_1\mathbf{z}) \]

Background. Image \(\mathbf{X}_v\) → vision tower features → two-layer MLP connector with GELU (Appendix A) → visual tokens \(\mathbf{H}_v\) in the LLM's embedding size (biases omitted).

Guide

The paper has no equations, so this one is background that describes Appendix A precisely. X sub v is the image, f sub VT is the vision tower, and g sub phi is the connector: a first weight matrix, a GELU nonlinearity, then a second weight matrix. The output H sub v is a row of visual tokens sized like the language model's word embeddings. Use it to explain the image path in your own words.

(B2)\[ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\sum_{i=1}^{L} m_i \,\log p_\theta\big(x_i \mid \mathbf{H}_v,\, x_{\lt i}\big), \qquad m_i = \begin{cases} 1 & x_i \in \text{answer} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

Background. Next-token loss over the conversation, counted only on answer tokens (the labels made by the chat template); \(\theta\) = whatever the recipe leaves trainable.

Guide

Also background, not from the paper. The loss is the usual next-token loss: the negative sum of log probabilities of each token given the visual tokens and all earlier tokens. The mask m sub i is one on answer tokens and zero elsewhere, which is what the chat template's labels do. Theta is whatever the training recipe leaves trainable, so the same loss serves full tuning and LoRA.

(B3)\[ \mathbf{W}' = \mathbf{W}_0 + \tfrac{\alpha}{r}\,\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}, \qquad \mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r},\ \mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times k},\ r \ll \min(d,k) \]

Background. LoRA recipe: frozen weight \(\mathbf{W}_0\) plus a trainable rank-\(r\) update; the QLoRA recipe stores \(\mathbf{W}_0\) in 4 bits (see the QLoRA tab).

Guide

The third background line is the LoRA update behind the codebase's lora and qlora recipes. W zero is a frozen weight, B times A is a small rank r correction, and alpha over r scales it. With QLoRA, W zero is stored in four bits. Only A and B are trained, which is why fine-tuning fits on a free GPU. The QLoRA tab explains the four-bit part in full.

Guide

This is the menu of parts the codebase ships: six small language models from 450 million to 2.7 billion parameters, four vision towers, five connector types, and recipes from frozen to full tuning, including LoRA and QLoRA. When you pick a model for your project, pick from this list, and note that Qwen 1.5 appears here but was not in the results table.

The authors report that these reproductions are slightly better overall than the original TinyLLaVA paper (trained with the LLaVA code); they attribute part of it to setting the image aspect ratio to "square" with SigLIP. Training details (Appendix A): one epoch per stage; base pre-train lr 1e-3, batch 256; SFT lr 2e-5, batch 128; share pre-train lr 2e-5, batch 256.

§8Putting it into practice

Using TinyLLaVA Factory for a text + image + voice task

  • Inputs: text and one image natively; no voice, no video, no speech output. Add a small open speech-to-text model (for example a Whisper variant) in front: transcribe the spoken question, then feed the transcript through the LLM's chat template together with the image.
  • Size: the smallest LLM in the paper is OpenELM-450M (Table 1, with CLIP or SigLIP), then TinyLlama-1.1B. With QLoRA a model in this range should plausibly fit a free Colab T4 (16 GB), and even the Phi-2-2.7B variant may fit in 4 bits, but the paper reports no memory figures: check the released checkpoints and their sizes on the project's model hub, and use fp16 on a T4 (no bf16).
  • Where to put LoRA: copy the paper's fine-tuning stage: keep the vision tower frozen, keep or fully train the small connector, and put LoRA / QLoRA adapters on the LLM (the codebase ships lora and qlora recipes, but the paper gives no LoRA hyperparameters or results, so report yours).
  • Task: the paper evaluates image question answering (VQAv2, GQA, ScienceQA-IMG, TextVQA). A natural fit is spoken questions about a photo or document image, answered in short text; convert your data into the LLaVA conversation format.
  • Fairness and normalization: errors can enter at the ASR step before the vision-language model sees anything, so compare accuracy for two speaker groups (for example male vs female voices, or Arabic-accented vs native English speech) and separate ASR errors from answer errors. For normalization, the ASR output's casing, punctuation and number format ("7" vs "seven") must be normalised consistently in both training labels and scoring.
Guide

Turn this box into your plan. The model reads text and one image, so add a speech-to-text model for voice and feed its transcript through the chat template. Start from the smallest variant, check its real size before training, and use fp16 on a T4. Freeze the vision tower and put LoRA on the language model. Then measure fairness across speaker groups, separating speech recognition errors from answer errors, and normalise transcripts the same way in training and scoring.

Seeing: vision-language models

SmolVLM: Redefining small and efficient multimodal models

Andrés Marafioti, Orr Zohar, Miquel Farré, Merve Noyan, Elie Bakouch, Pedro Cuenca, Cyril Zakka, Loubna Ben Allal, Anton Lozhkov, Nouamane Tazi, Vaibhav Srivastav, Joshua Lochner, Hugo Larcher, Mathieu Morlon, Lewis Tunstall, Leandro von Werra, Thomas Wolf · Hugging Face / Stanford University · arXiv 2504.05299v1, April 2025

SmolVLM is a family of tiny open vision-language models (256M, 500M and 2.2B parameters) that read text, single or multiple images and video, and answer in text. Instead of shrinking a big VLM, the authors re-tune every design choice for small scale: a small SigLIP image encoder, a longer context, aggressive pixel-shuffle compression of visual tokens, image splitting, learned tile-position tokens, and a carefully balanced training mix. The 256M model runs in under 1 GB of GPU memory. There is no audio input and no speech output.

Variants
256M · 500M · 2.2B
Inputs
text · image · multi-image · video (no audio)
Vision encoder
SigLIP-B/16 93M · SO400M 428M
Language model
SmolLM2 135M · 360M · 1.7B
GPU RAM, batch 1
0.8 · 1.2 · 4.9 GB
Avg. score (Table 1)
44.0 · 51.0 · 59.8 %
Reading guide

SmolVLM asks how small a vision-language model can be while still reading documents, charts and videos well, and why small models built by shrinking big ones waste so much memory. Its answer is to redesign every choice for small scale: a small image encoder, a longer context, very aggressive compression of image tokens, image splitting, learned tile-position tokens and a carefully balanced data mix. The smallest model, with 256 million parameters, runs in under one gigabyte of GPU memory. The tab moves from the big picture and the problem, through the method, the few key relations, every figure and the results tables, to a box on using SmolVLM in practice. Among the eleven papers it is the third, after QLoRA and TinyLLaVA Factory, and the last pure vision model before the speech papers, starting with Voxtral. Keep in mind that it accepts text, images and video, but no voice.

§0Before you read

To follow SmolVLM you need one idea above all: a picture reaches a language model as a row of tokens, and every token costs memory and context space. The paper is about spending as few tokens as possible per image so that a tiny model can still read documents and watch videos. It is in the atlas because its 256M and 500M models are among the easiest image-and-text models to fine-tune with LoRA on a free T4, although it has no voice input.

Terms used in this paper

Vision-language model (VLM)
A model that takes images (or video) plus text and answers in text. It joins a vision encoder to a language model through a projector.
Token and context window
A token is one unit the language model reads, such as a word piece or one visual feature. The context window is the maximum number of tokens it can read at once.
Vision transformer (ViT) and patch
A ViT cuts an image into small square patches (here 16 × 16 pixels) and turns each patch into one feature vector.
SigLIP
A family of image encoders trained to match images with captions using a sigmoid loss. SmolVLM uses SigLIP-B/16 (93M parameters) and the larger SigLIP-SO400M (about 400M).
SmolLM2
Hugging Face's small open language models with 135M, 360M and 1.7B parameters; they are the text backbone of the three SmolVLM sizes.
Projector
A small MLP that maps visual features into the same vector size as the language model's word embeddings, so they can sit in one sequence.
Pixel shuffle
Also called space-to-depth: it stacks each \(r \times r\) block of neighbouring features into one position, cutting the number of visual tokens by \(r^2\) without discarding values.
Image splitting
Cutting a high-resolution image into sub-image tiles plus one downsized global view, so small text stays readable at the encoder's input size.
RoPE
Rotary position embedding: it tells the model where each token sits by rotating its vectors. Raising its base (here from 10k to 273k) helps the model handle longer contexts.
OCR
Optical character recognition: reading printed or handwritten text in an image. Documents, charts and screenshots all need it.
OCRBench, DocVQA, ChartQA
Benchmarks that test reading text in images, answering questions about document scans, and answering questions about charts.
MMMU and MathVista
Image-question benchmarks that need reasoning: MMMU uses college-level questions across many subjects, MathVista mathematical questions about figures.
Video-MME
A video understanding benchmark with multiple-choice questions about short, medium and long videos.
A100, L4 and WebGPU
The A100 is a large NVIDIA data-centre GPU and the L4 a smaller, cheaper one. WebGPU lets a web browser use the computer's GPU, so a model can run inside a web page.
Guide

These are the terms the paper uses without explaining. The most important are pixel shuffle, which cuts visual tokens by the square of its ratio, the context window, which is how many tokens the model can read at once, and SigLIP and SmolLM2, the vision encoder and language model inside SmolVLM. The benchmark names at the end, such as OCRBench, MMMU and Video-MME, appear in the results table.

§2Big picture

SmolVLM keeps the standard "encoder + projector + LLM" layout (as in Idefics3) and wins by making every part fit a small model.

The key trick is spending very few tokens per image, so a 135M to 1.7B language model can still attend over many tiles or frames.

§3The problem

  • Small VLMs usually copy big-model choices, such as many image tokens per picture, so memory stays high (Qwen2-VL-2B needs 13.7 GB, InternVL2-2B 10.5 GB).
  • A 2k context cannot hold even two uncompressed image tiles plus text.
  • Small models are fragile in training: string position tags cause the "OCR loss plague", and data recipes from big LLMs (SFT text, heavy chain-of-thought) hurt them.

§4Method

  1. Balance the towers. Pair small SmolLM2 models (135M, 360M) with the 93M SigLIP-B/16; use the 428M SigLIP-SO400M only with the 1.7B LM (Finding 1).
  2. Extend the context. Raise the RoPE base from 10k to 273k and fine-tune on long (Dolma books, The Stack) plus short text; use 16k tokens for the 2.2B model and 8k for the smaller ones (Finding 2).
  3. Compress visual tokens. Pixel shuffle (space-to-depth) folds r × r neighbouring features into one token, cutting tokens by r². Small models prefer the aggressive r = 4 (Finding 3).
  4. Split images, not videos. High-resolution images become sub-image tiles plus a downsized global image; video frames are rescaled to the encoder resolution, with no frame averaging (Finding 4).
  5. Mark tile positions with learned tokens instead of strings like <row_1_col_2> typed as text (Finding 5).
  6. Structure the prompt. Add a system prompt and media intro/outro text ("Here is an image...", "Given this image..."), and mask the user prompt so the loss is only on completions (Finding 6).
  7. Curate the data. Keep about 14% text but do not reuse LLM-SFT text (SmolTalk), add only a tiny fraction of chain-of-thought, and train on videos averaging about 3.5 minutes (Findings 7–9).
  8. Train in two stages: a vision stage (images + text), then a video stage (video, image, multi-image and text).
Guide

These eight steps are the whole SmolVLM recipe in order of the paper. The first four are architecture: balance encoder and language model, stretch the context, compress image tokens, and split images but not videos. The next two are about how the input is written: learned tile tokens and a structured prompt with loss only on answers. The last two are about data and training stages. Each step is backed by one of the nine findings in the table below.

Forward pass (reconstructed from §2–§3; the paper has no algorithm box) input : text prompt t, images I_1..I_k or video V for each image I: tiles = split(I) + [downsize(I)] # sub-images + global view for video V: tiles = sample_frames(V), rescaled to encoder size # no frame averaging seq = [system prompt] + tokenize(t_before) for each tile j: F = SigLIP(tile_j) # (H/p) x (W/p) x d patch features F' = pixel_shuffle(F, r) # (H/pr) x (W/pr) x d r^2 V_j = MLP(F') # visual tokens in LLM width seq += [intro text if j == 0] + [pos_token_j] + V_j seq += [outro text] + tokenize(question) answer = SmolLM2.generate(seq) # text only
Guide

This pseudo-code is reconstructed from sections two and three, because the paper has no algorithm box. Follow the flow: every image becomes tiles plus a global view, every video becomes sampled frames, each tile goes through the encoder, pixel shuffle and projector, and the resulting visual tokens are placed in the sequence after a tile-position token, wrapped by intro and outro text. The language model then generates text only.

Guide

The paper is organised as nine findings, each a short rule for small multimodal models, and this table maps each one to the figure that supports it. Findings one to four are about architecture, five and six about how inputs and prompts are tokenized, and seven to nine about training data. Use it as a checklist when you design your own fine-tuning setup.

§5Every equation

The paper has no numbered equations and no display math. The relations below are stated in words in the text (or are the standard forms behind them); they are labelled A–E rather than numbered.

(A)\[ N_{\text{patch}} = \frac{H}{p}\cdot\frac{W}{p}, \qquad \frac{512}{16}\cdot\frac{512}{16} = 1024 \]

Patch tokens from a ViT encoder with patch size \(p\): a 512 × 512 image through SigLIP-B/16 gives 1,024 tokens (§2.2).

Guide

N patch equals H over p times W over p: the number of image tokens a vision transformer produces is the image height divided by the patch size, times the width divided by the patch size. For a 512 pixel image and SigLIP's patch size of 16, that is 32 times 32, or 1,024 tokens. This number is why image tokens flood a small context.

(B)\[ \mathbf{F}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times w\times d}\;\longmapsto\;\mathbf{F}'\in\mathbb{R}^{\frac{h}{r}\times\frac{w}{r}\times d\,r^{2}}, \qquad N_{\text{vis}} = \frac{N_{\text{patch}}}{r^{2}} \]

Pixel shuffle (space-to-depth) with ratio \(r\): each \(r\times r\) block of features becomes one token with \(r^2\) times more channels, so the token count drops by \(r^2\) (§2.2, Fig. 4).

Guide

Pixel shuffle rearranges a feature map of height h, width w and d channels into one of height h over r, width w over r and d times r squared channels. Nothing is thrown away, but the number of positions, which are the visual tokens, falls by a factor of r squared. With r equal to four that is a sixteen-fold cut. This is the paper's main compression tool.

(C)\[ N_{\text{vis}} = \frac{1024}{4^{2}} = 64 \ \text{tokens per 512}\times\text{512 tile at } r=4 \]

Derived from (A) and (B) for the small variants with r = 4; the paper does not print this number.

Guide

Putting the two relations together: 1,024 patch tokens divided by four squared gives 64 visual tokens for each 512 pixel tile at a shuffle ratio of four. The paper does not print this number, so treat it as a derived estimate for the small variants. It explains why the language model can afford many tiles or frames.

(D)\[ \theta_i = b^{-2i/d_{\text{head}}}, \qquad b:\ 10\,000 \;\rightarrow\; 273\,000 \]

Standard RoPE frequencies; the paper only states that the base \(b\) was raised from 10k to 273k to extend the context to 8k–16k tokens (§2.2).

Guide

Rotary position embeddings rotate each pair of dimensions at a frequency theta i, equal to the base b raised to minus two i over the head dimension. The paper raises the base b from ten thousand to 273 thousand, which slows the rotations so the model can tell apart positions over a much longer sequence. This is how SmolLM2's context grew from two thousand to eight or sixteen thousand tokens.

(E)\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}} = -\sum_{t} m_t \,\log p_\theta\!\left(y_t \mid y_{\lt t}\right), \qquad m_t = \begin{cases}1 & y_t \in \text{completion}\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases} \]

User-prompt masking (§3.2, Finding 6: "only train on completions"): the next-token loss counts only assistant answer tokens. Standard form; the paper describes it in words.

Guide

The fine-tuning loss is the usual next-token loss, minus the log probability of each token y t given the tokens before it, but multiplied by a mask m t. The mask is one for tokens in the assistant's answer and zero everywhere else. So the model is never trained to reproduce the question or the image tokens. The paper states this in words as Finding 6, and it is the setting you should use.

§8Putting it into practice

Using SmolVLM for a text + image + voice task

  • Inputs: text native, image and multi-image native, video native, voice not supported. SmolVLM has no audio encoder and produces only text, so put a small open speech-to-text model (for example a Whisper checkpoint) in front and feed its transcript into the user turn next to the image.
  • Size: the smallest release, SmolVLM-256M, needs about 0.8 GB for inference (500M: 1.2 GB), so LoRA or QLoRA on a free Colab T4 (16 GB) is very plausible, even alongside the ASR model. The 2.2B model (4.9 GB at inference) should fit with QLoRA, but check: image splitting at high resolution makes long sequences, so reduce the image size or number of tiles if memory runs out. The paper itself reports no fine-tuning memory numbers.
  • Where to put LoRA: on the SmolLM2 attention and MLP projections (the language backbone), keeping the SigLIP encoder frozen; the small MLP projector can optionally be trained. This is a common recipe, not something the paper tests.
  • What the paper suggests for the task: keep its chat format (system prompt, "Here is an image..." intro/outro, learned tile tokens handled by the processor), and mask the user prompt so the loss is only on answers (Finding 6). Keep some text-only examples, avoid adding lots of chain-of-thought, and prefer the r = 4, split-image setup the model was trained with. A good fit is spoken questions about documents or charts, which match its OCR-heavy training data (Fig. 8).
  • Normalization and fairness angle: ASR transcripts differ from typed questions in casing, punctuation and number format ("twenty five" vs "25"), and exact-match style answers (DocVQA, ChartQA) are sensitive to the same; normalize both and measure the effect. For fairness, compare accuracy for male vs female or accented speakers, where ASR errors propagate into the VLM. The paper reports only English benchmarks, so Arabic performance is unknown and worth testing.
Guide

This box turns the paper into practical decisions. SmolVLM covers text and images natively but has no voice input, so plan a speech-to-text model in front of it. The 256 million or 500 million model fits a free T4 comfortably; the 2.2 billion model probably fits with QLoRA, but check memory. Put LoRA on the language backbone, keep the paper's prompt format and answer-only loss, and use transcript normalization and speaker groups for your experiments.

Hearing: speech-language models

Voxtral

Alexander H. Liu, Andy Ehrenberg, Andy Lo, Clément Denoix, … Mistral AI · arXiv 2507.13264 · July 2025 · Apache 2.0

Voxtral bolts a Whisper speech encoder onto a Mistral language model so the model can listen as well as read. A small MLP adapter squeezes the 50 Hz audio embeddings down 4× to 12.5 Hz, so 40 minutes of speech fit in a 32K context next to the text prompt. The output is always text: answers, transcripts, translations or function calls. There is no image input and no speech output.

Reading guide

Voxtral asks how to give a text language model good ears without hurting what it already knows. Mistral's answer is simple: put a Whisper speech encoder in front of a Mistral decoder, compress the audio four times with a small adapter, and train on audio and text together. The tab starts with the big picture of every input path, then the problems of long audio and synthetic speech, the method and training recipe, the few relations the paper states in prose, all nine figures redrawn, the eight tables, and finally a box on using Voxtral in your own project. In the atlas this is the first paper of the hearing group. It comes after QLoRA, TinyLLaVA Factory and SmolVLM, which cover fine-tuning and vision, and before Voxtral Realtime, LFM2 and the omni models that combine all three senses.

§0Before you read

Voxtral is the atlas's first model that listens: it turns speech into tokens that a Mistral language model reads next to your text prompt, and it answers in text. To follow it you need three ideas: how sound becomes tokens, how speech output is scored with word error rate, and which parts you would freeze or train. It is a strong candidate for the voice part of a text, image and voice project, but it has no image input.

Terms used in this paper

Speech-language model
A language model that also accepts audio as input. Voxtral listens and reads, but always answers in text.
Log-Mel spectrogram
A picture of sound: time runs left to right, pitch bands bottom to top, brightness is loudness. Here 128 bands, 100 frames per second.
Whisper large-v3
OpenAI's open speech-recognition model. Voxtral reuses only its encoder (about 640M parameters), which hears 30 seconds at a time.
Adapter (downsampling)
A small MLP between encoder and LLM that joins every 4 audio frames into one token, from 50 to 12.5 per second.
Context window (32K)
The most tokens the LLM can read at once, here about 32,000. At 12.5 audio tokens per second that is about 40 minutes of speech.
Ministral 3B / Mistral Small 3.1
The text-only Mistral LLMs used as decoders: Ministral 3B for Voxtral Mini (4.7B in total), Mistral Small 3.1 (24B) for Voxtral Small.
ASR
Automatic speech recognition: turning speech into a written transcript. Voxtral has a dedicated transcribe mode for it.
WER
Word error rate: substitutions plus deletions plus insertions, divided by the number of reference words. Lower is better.
BLEU
A 0 to 100 score for translation that counts word sequences shared with a reference translation. Higher is better.
FLEURS / Common Voice
Multilingual speech test sets: FLEURS has read sentences in about 100 languages; Mozilla Common Voice is crowd-recorded. Both include Arabic and English.
TTS
Text-to-speech. The authors made spoken training questions and spoken versions of text benchmarks by reading text aloud with a TTS engine.
Diarization / VAD
Voice activity detection finds where speech is; diarization labels who speaks when. Used to cut long recordings into audio and text pairs.
DPO / Online DPO
Direct preference optimization: train on a preferred and a rejected answer to the same prompt. In Online DPO the pairs are fresh samples from the current model.
Guide

These are the words the paper uses without explaining them. Read log-Mel spectrogram, adapter and context window first, because they explain how audio fits into a language model. WER and BLEU are the scores in the results tables, FLEURS and Common Voice are the speech test sets, and TTS, diarization and DPO describe how the training data and preference tuning were built.

§2Big picture

Speech is turned into “audio tokens” that the LLM reads exactly like word embeddings. The trick that makes long audio affordable is the adapter: 4× fewer audio tokens with no loss in understanding. Images and video have no path at all.

§3The problem

  • An audio encoder produces a vector every 20 ms (50 Hz), while a text token covers roughly a word: long audio explodes the sequence length and memory.
  • Whisper has a fixed 30-second receptive field, so arbitrary-length audio needs a chunking scheme.
  • Adding speech must not damage the text skills of the backbone LLM.
  • Existing speech benchmarks mostly test transcription and translation, not understanding or reasoning.

§4Method

How speech becomes tokens

Training recipe: what is trained when

  1. Segment. Long recordings are cut into audio–text pairs \((A_n,T_n)\) using voice-activity detection and diarization; missing transcripts are pseudo-labelled with an ASR model.
  2. Warm-up. One pass over the data mixture trains only the adapter (encoder and decoder frozen).
  3. Pretrain with two patterns, 50 : 50. Repetition \(A_n \to T_n\) (signalled by <repeat>) teaches transcription; cross-modal continuation \(A_1,T_2,A_3,T_4,\dots\) (signalled by <next>) teaches the model to keep a conversation going across modalities. Text-only pretraining data is mixed in to keep text skills.
  4. Supervised fine-tuning. (a) long audio as context + text question, with QA pairs written by Mistral Large from transcripts, plus summaries and translations; (b) audio-only questions: TTS versions of text SFT data (including function calling) plus real human spoken questions; (c) a dedicated transcribe mode token that removes the need for a text prompt.
  5. Preference alignment. DPO and Online DPO: two samples at temperature 0.5, audio replaced by its transcript, ranked by a text reward model.
Guide

The recipe has five stages that move from alignment to behaviour. First, long recordings are split into matched audio and text pieces. Then a warm up trains only the adapter. Pretraining mixes two patterns half and half, one teaching transcription and one teaching the model to carry context across speech and text. Supervised fine-tuning adds question answering, spoken instructions and a transcribe mode. Preference alignment with DPO finally polishes the answers.

Supervised fine-tuning data

Preference alignment

Evaluation recipe (speech-synthesized benchmarks and SU benchmark)

  1. Filter. An LLM labels each text prompt from GSM8K, TriviaQA and MMLU as verbalizable, verbalizable with rewrite, or non-verbalizable (tables, figures, long code are dropped).
  2. Normalize for speech (App. A.3, paraphrased): numbers written as words, Roman numerals after names read as ordinals, acronyms spelled out, bullets turned into “first, second…”, markdown symbols removed, links read out, sentences kept under 250 characters.
  3. Synthesize. Each prompt is spoken by a TTS engine with a speaker embedding sampled from a diverse pool of single-speaker 6-second clips.
  4. Score. Outputs are text, so the original scoring applies. For the internal SU benchmark (audio up to 19 min) an LLM judge sees the transcript, question, reference and answer.
Guide

Mistral built new benchmarks by turning text tests into speech. An LLM first sorts each question from GSM8K, TriviaQA and MMLU into speakable, speakable after rewriting, or unspeakable. The rewrite rules are really text normalization: numbers become words, acronyms are spelled out and markdown is removed. A synthetic voice then reads each question with a randomly chosen speaker. These rules are a ready checklist for a text normalization experiment.

SU judge (App. A.4, schematic) for each (audio, question, reference, candidate): transcript = ASR(audio) # judge never hears audio repeat 10 times: binary = judge(transcript, question, reference, candidate) # 1 = correct and helpful grade = judge(..., scale = 0..5) # 5 = correct, well presented report mean ± std over trials of % binary and mean grade
Guide

The internal speech understanding benchmark is scored by an LLM judge that never hears the audio. For every answer, the judge reads the transcript, the question, a reference answer and the candidate. It gives a one or zero for correct and helpful, and a grade from zero to five. Each answer is judged ten times and the mean and standard deviation are reported. Table 2 uses exactly these two scores.

§5Every equation

The paper contains no numbered equations. Below are the quantitative relations it states in prose, written as math so you can reuse them; items marked “background” are standard formulas the paper cites but does not print.

(u1)\[ 100\ \text{Hz (log-Mel, hop 160)} \xrightarrow{\ \text{conv stem } \div 2\ } 50\ \text{Hz} \xrightarrow{\ \text{MLP adapter } \div 4\ } 12.5\ \text{Hz} \]

Audio frame-rate chain (§2.1–2.2). The 100 Hz spectrogram rate follows from hop 160 at Whisper’s 16 kHz sampling; the paper states the 50 Hz and 12.5 Hz values.

Guide

Audio moves through three frame rates. The log Mel spectrogram, with a hop of 160 samples, has 100 frames per second. Whisper's convolution stem halves that to 50, and the MLP adapter divides by four to reach 12.5 audio tokens per second. The paper states the 50 and 12.5 values; the 100 follows from Whisper's 16 kilohertz input. Figure 8 is the experiment that justifies stopping at 12.5.

(u2)\[ N_{\text{audio}} = r \cdot t,\qquad 50 \times 1800\,\text{s} = 90{,}000,\qquad 12.5 \times 2400\,\text{s} = 30{,}000 \le 32{,}768 \]

Audio tokens = frame rate \(r\) × duration \(t\): 30 min at 50 Hz is 90k tokens; 40 min at 12.5 Hz fits a 32K context.

Guide

The number of audio tokens is simply the frame rate r times the duration t in seconds. Thirty minutes at 50 per second gives 90 thousand tokens, far beyond the context. Forty minutes at 12.5 per second gives 30 thousand, which fits under 32 thousand 768. This one line is the reason the adapter exists, and you can use the same arithmetic to budget memory for your own clips.

(u3)\[ t_{\text{pad}} = 30\left\lceil t/30 \right\rceil \ \text{s},\qquad N_{\text{chunks}} = \left\lceil t/30 \right\rceil,\qquad 30\,\text{s} \mapsto 375 \text{ audio tokens} \]

Every clip is padded to the next multiple of 30 s and split into chunks encoded independently (§2.1, §5.1).

Guide

Every clip is padded up to the next multiple of 30 seconds, and the number of chunks is the duration divided by 30, rounded up. Each chunk becomes 375 audio tokens. So a five second voice question still costs a full 375 tokens, which matters for GPU memory on a free T4. Figure 7 tests whether this padding could be dropped, and the answer was no.

(u4)\[ \text{repeat: } \langle\text{bos}\rangle\, A_n\, \langle\text{repeat}\rangle\, T_n\, \langle\text{eos}\rangle \]

Audio-to-text repetition pattern: audio segment \(A_n\) followed by its own transcript \(T_n\) (§3.1, Fig. 2).

Guide

The repetition pattern is a speech recognition lesson. A training sequence starts with a begin token, then the audio segment A n, then the repeat token, then its own transcript T n, and an end token. The model learns to write down exactly what it heard. Figure 9 shows that this pattern alone gives low word error rates but almost no question answering ability.

(u5)\[ \text{continuation: } (A_1, T_2, A_3, T_4, \dots, A_{N-1}, T_N),\ \ \langle\text{next}\rangle \text{ before each switch} \]

Cross-modal continuation: each audio segment is followed by the next text segment \(T_{n+1}\); the two patterns are sampled with probability 0.5 each.

Guide

The continuation pattern alternates modalities: audio one, then text two, then audio three, then text four, and so on. Each audio segment is followed by the next piece of text rather than its own transcript, marked by the next token. This teaches the model to keep a conversation going across speech and text. Half of pretraining uses this pattern and half uses repetition.

(u6)\[ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\sum_{i} \log p_\theta\!\left(y_i \mid y_{\lt i},\ \mathbf{a},\ \mathbf{x}\right) \]

Implied objective (Fig. 1: “auto-regressively predicts text tokens, conditional on the audio and text inputs”): next-token loss on text tokens \(y\) given audio tokens \(\mathbf{a}\) and text \(\mathbf{x}\).

Guide

The training objective is ordinary next token prediction on text. The loss is minus the sum of the log probabilities of each text token y i, given the earlier tokens, the audio tokens a and the text prompt x. The paper does not print this formula, but Figure 1 describes exactly this. Your LoRA fine-tuning uses the same loss, usually computed only on the answer tokens.

(bg)\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}} = -\log \sigma\!\left(\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w\mid x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l\mid x)}\right) \]

Background (Rafailov et al., not printed in the paper): DPO raises the likelihood of the preferred answer \(y_w\) over the rejected \(y_l\) relative to a frozen reference \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\); in Online DPO both come from the current policy at \(T=0.5\).

Guide

DPO is background here; the paper cites it but does not print it. The loss compares how much the model, relative to a frozen reference, prefers the chosen answer y w over the rejected answer y l, scaled by beta and passed through a sigmoid. Minimising it makes good answers more likely without training a separate reward model. In Voxtral's online variant, both answers are fresh samples from the current model.

(u7)\[ 640\text{M} + 25\text{M} + 400\text{M} + 3.6\text{B} \approx 4.7\text{B (Mini)},\qquad 640\text{M} + 52\text{M} + 670\text{M} + 22.9\text{B} \approx 24.3\text{B (Small)} \]

Parameter budget (Table 1): audio encoder + adapter + text embeddings + decoder.

Guide

The parameter budget adds four parts: the 640 million parameter Whisper encoder, the small adapter, the text embedding table and the decoder. Voxtral Mini totals about 4.7 billion and Small about 24.3 billion. The encoder is the same in both, and the adapter is under one percent of the total. For your GPU budget, Mini is the one to consider.
