§8Putting it into practice

Using Voxtral in your own project

  • Inputs: text and speech natively (speech in, text out). No image input and no speech output. For a text + image + voice task, add a small vision model in a pipeline, for example image → caption or OCR text from a small VLM (such as SmolVLM in this atlas), then feed that text plus the spoken question to Voxtral.
  • Size: the smallest release is Voxtral Mini (Ministral 3B decoder, 4.7B parameters in total including the 640M Whisper encoder). In 4-bit QLoRA it plausibly fits a free T4 (16 GB) with batch size 1, short clips and gradient checkpointing, but check: every clip is padded to 30 s, which is 375 audio tokens per 30-second chunk, and the T4 has no bf16 (use fp16 compute). Voxtral Small (24.3B) will not fit.
  • Where to put LoRA: on the language decoder’s attention and MLP projections; keep the Whisper encoder frozen. The adapter (25M) is small enough to train fully; the paper’s own warm-up trained only the adapter, which shows it is the cheapest bridge between audio and text.
  • What the paper suggests for your data: copy its SFT recipe. Use “audio as context + text question” and “spoken question, text answer” examples, generate question–answer pairs from transcripts with an LLM, and include real human recordings, since TTS-only questions generalised poorly to accented speech. For a pure ASR sub-task, use the transcribe mode instead of a prompt.
  • Fairness and normalization: Arabic vs English is a built-in fairness split (FLEURS WER 13.4 vs 3.4 for Small, 25.4 vs 3.8 for Mini). The App. A.3 rewrite rules (numbers as words, spelled-out acronyms, no markdown) are a ready list of text-normalization steps; WER changes with normalization, and the paper does not state which WER normalizer it used, so apply one consistently to references and outputs.
Guide

Use this box as the plan for your project. Voxtral handles your voice and text inputs natively, so the only extra piece is a small vision model that turns the image into text. Start from Voxtral Mini in four bit, put LoRA on the decoder projections, keep Whisper frozen, and check memory with 30 second padded clips on a T4. Build the dataset the way the paper did, with some real human recordings, and use Arabic against English as your fairness split.

Hearing: speech-language models

Voxtral Realtime

Mistral AI (core contributors: Alexander H. Liu, Andy Ehrenberg, Andy Lo, Chen-Yo Sun, Guillaume Lample, et al.) · technical report, arXiv 2602.11298 (v3, Apr 2026)

A 4B speech-to-text model that transcribes while you are still speaking. Audio goes through a causal encoder, is squeezed to one embedding per 80 ms, added to the last text token, and a language decoder emits one token per frame: a “wait” token until a word is heard, then the word. One knob, the delay τ, trades speed for accuracy; at 480 ms it is about as accurate as offline Whisper.

Size
4.4B (0.97B enc + 3.4B dec)
Input → output
speech → text only
Delay knob τ
80–2400 ms, step 80
FLEURS WER @480 ms
8.72% (Whisper 8.23%)
Languages
13 (incl. Arabic)
Weights
Apache 2.0 · Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime-2602
Reading guide

Voxtral Realtime asks whether a speech recognizer can write text while you are still talking and still be as accurate as a model that waits for the whole recording. Its answer is yes: a 4.4 billion parameter model with a causal audio encoder and a language decoder that emits one token every 80 milliseconds, matching offline Whisper at a delay of 480 milliseconds. The tab moves from the big picture and the problem to the method, the equations, all five figures, the eight results tables, and a box on what this means for your own project. When choosing models, remember the short version: it hears speech and writes text, and nothing else. Among the eleven papers in this atlas it sits in the hearing group, right after Voxtral and before LFM2. It follows QLoRA, TinyLLaVA Factory and SmolVLM, and the omni models later in the atlas take the same audio ideas further.

§0Before you read

Voxtral Realtime is a speech recognizer that writes the transcript while you are still speaking, a few hundred milliseconds behind your voice. To follow it you need three ideas: what streaming and delay mean, how a waveform becomes one vector every 80 ms, and how transcripts are scored with word error rate. For a text, image and voice project it is a speech-in, text-out stage you can put in front of a vision-language model, and its Arabic versus English results are a ready-made fairness comparison.

Terms used in this paper

ASR (speech-to-text)
Automatic speech recognition: turning spoken audio into written text. Voxtral Realtime does only this.
Offline vs streaming
Offline models read the whole recording before writing. Streaming models write while audio is still arriving, so they cannot use future sound.
Delay \( \tau \)
How far the transcript lags behind the speaker. The paper tests 80 ms to 2400 ms in steps of 80 ms; one model handles all of them.
log-Mel spectrogram
A picture of sound: energy in 128 pitch bands, measured every 10 ms, on a log scale. The standard input to speech encoders.
Causal attention
Each position may look only at itself and earlier positions. Needed for streaming; offline encoders like Whisper's are bidirectional.
Adapter
A small MLP that stacks four 20 ms encoder vectors into one 80 ms vector the size of the decoder's token embeddings.
[P] and [W] tokens
Special outputs: [P] means "nothing to write yet"; [W] marks the start of a word (or group of words) that follows as normal subword tokens.
Ada RMS-Norm
The paper's way of telling the decoder the chosen delay: a small network turns \( \tau \) into a vector that rescales each block's normalised feed-forward input.
KV cache
Stored attention keys and values of past positions, so each new 80 ms step reuses earlier work. The paper serves the model with vLLM, which manages this cache.
WER / CER
Word (or character) error rate: substitutions, deletions and insertions divided by reference length. Lower is better.
FLEURS
A multilingual benchmark of read Wikipedia sentences in about 100 languages; the paper uses 13 of them, including Arabic.
Mozilla Common Voice (MCV)
Crowd-sourced recordings by volunteers on their own microphones; noisier and harder than FLEURS.
Whisper
OpenAI's widely used offline speech recognizer, the main accuracy baseline. Voxtral Realtime roughly matches it at 480 ms delay.
DSM
Delayed Streams Modeling (Kyutai, 2025): a decoder-only model reads audio and text streams side by side, with text shifted by a delay. Voxtral Realtime builds on this design.
Guide

These are the words the paper uses without explaining. The most important are delay, which is how far the transcript lags behind the voice, causal attention, which means looking only at the past, and word error rate, the score in every table. FLEURS and Common Voice are the two multilingual test sets, and Whisper is the offline baseline the paper tries to match. Come back here whenever a term in the tab stops you.

§1Big picture

Streaming is built in from training, not bolted on afterwards. For a text, image and voice project this makes Voxtral Realtime a speech-to-text front end, not a full text + image + voice model.

§2The problem

  • Chunked offline models degrade most at low delay and out of distribution.
  • Transducers (RNN-T) and DSM stream natively, but before this paper none reached offline accuracy at sub-second delay across many languages.
  • DSM also needs a separate way to tell the model the target delay; the paper finds better ways than adding it to the input (Fig. 3).

§3Method

3.1 Audio path: causal encoder and adapter

3.2 Delay conditioning with Ada RMS-Norm

3.3 Training targets: [P] and [W]

3.4 Training recipe

  1. Build targets. From (audio, transcript, word timestamps), write one token per 80 ms frame: [P], or [W] + subwords once a word is complete and τ has elapsed; group words that share an emission frame.
  2. Sample a delay per example. τ uniform in 80…2400 ms (1–30 frames); feed it through g(τ) into every decoder block.
  3. Initialise. Encoder and adapter random; decoder from Ministral 3B.
  4. Warm up the encoder (5%). Decoder frozen; encoder + adapter trained with AdamW, lr 4 × 10⁻⁴.
  5. Train end-to-end (95%). All weights, lr 6 × 10⁻⁵, batch 370 hours of audio, plus z-loss on logits to stop audio being ignored.
  6. Serve. vLLM with a paged KV cache for both encoder (50 Hz) and decoder (12.5 Hz), resumable streaming requests and a WebSocket API; optional left-padding of 16–32 silent frames at start (Table 4).
Guide

The procedure has a clear logic. First turn transcripts with word timestamps into frame by frame targets, so audio and text are aligned. Then give each example a random delay so one model learns them all. Initialise the decoder from a pretrained text model and the encoder from scratch, warm up the encoder while the decoder is frozen, and only then train end to end with a z loss. Serving comes last and adds engineering, not new learning.

3.5 Streaming inference loop

Streaming decode (our summary of §2–§4 and Fig. 5; the paper has no Algorithm box) input : audio stream, chosen delay τ (multiple of 80 ms), left-pad L frames state : encoder KV cache (50 Hz), decoder KV cache (12.5 Hz), 4-frame conv history prefill: audio = L zero frames + first τ ms ; text = ⟨bos⟩ + one [P] per prefill frame prev ← last prefill token loop every 80 ms: a ← adapter( encoder( next 80 ms of log-Mel, cached state ) ) # 4 enc frames → 1 z ← a + embed(prev) # fuse audio + text tok ← decoder(z, τ) # one token: [P] | [W] | subword if tok is a subword: output tok to the transcript prev ← tok # fed back next step (the resumable request)
Guide

This loop is our summary of how the model runs live, since the paper has no algorithm box. After a short prefill of silence and the first tau milliseconds of audio, every 80 milliseconds the encoder and adapter turn new sound into one embedding. It is added to the previous token, the decoder outputs one token, and only real subword tokens go to the transcript. The chosen token is fed back as the next step's text input, which is exactly the resumable request of Figure 5.

3.6 Serving detail: two KV caches at two rates

§4Every equation

The paper has no numbered equations. Its one display (the Ada RMS-Norm block) is given as (i)–(ii); (iii)–(v) write out quantities the paper states in words; (vi)–(viii) are standard definitions the paper uses but does not write (marked).

(i)\[ r_{\text{attn}} = \operatorname{Attn}\big(\operatorname{RMSNorm}(x)\big), \qquad h = x + r_{\text{attn}} \]

Attention sub-layer of every decoder block (paper display, §2.3). x = hidden states; no delay conditioning here.

Guide

This is the first half of every decoder block. The hidden state x is normalised with RMS norm, passed through attention, and the result r attn is added back to x to give h. Nothing about the delay enters here. The paper keeps the attention branch unconditioned on purpose, and the next equation shows where the delay goes instead.

(ii)\[ r_{\text{ffn}} = \operatorname{FFN}\big(\operatorname{RMSNorm}(h) \odot (1.0 + g(\tau))\big), \qquad y = h + r_{\text{ffn}} \]

Ada RMS-Norm: the normalised input to the feed-forward branch is scaled element-wise by 1 + g(τ). g(τ)=0 gives back a plain block.

Guide

This is the second half of the block and the heart of Ada RMS-Norm. The normalised h is multiplied element by element by one plus g of tau before the feed-forward network, and its output r f f n is added back to give y. If g of tau were zero, you would get an ordinary transformer block, so the delay acts as a gentle, learned rescaling of each feature.

(iii)\[ g(\tau) = \operatorname{MLP}_{\text{GELU}}\big(\operatorname{PE}_{\sin}(\tau)\big) \in \mathbb{R}^{d}, \quad \text{inner dim } 32,\ d = 3072 \]

Stated in words (§2.3): sinusoidal embedding of τ, small MLP with GELU. About 5M extra parameters in total.

Guide

This writes out in symbols what the paper says in words. The delay tau is encoded with sine and cosine waves, then a small MLP with a GELU activation and an inner width of only 32 maps it to a vector of size d, 3072 for this decoder. That vector is g of tau, used in equation two. The narrow inner width is why the whole mechanism adds only about five million parameters.

(iv)\[ \tau \sim \mathcal{U}\{80k\ \text{ms} : k = 1,\dots,30\} \]

Delay sampling during training (§3.2): 80 ms to 2400 ms in 80 ms steps, i.e. 1–30 adapter frames.

Guide

During training the delay is drawn uniformly from thirty values, 80 milliseconds times k, for k from one to thirty, so from 80 up to 2400 milliseconds. Each value is a whole number of 80 millisecond adapter frames. Because the model sees all of them, one set of weights can serve any of those delays at inference, which is what the latency curve in Figure 1 sweeps.

(v)\[ \frac{16\,000\ \text{Hz}}{160} = 100\ \text{Hz} \;\xrightarrow{\;\div 2\;}\; 50\ \text{Hz} \;\xrightarrow{\;\div 4\;}\; 12.5\ \text{Hz} = \frac{1}{80\ \text{ms}}, \qquad \frac{750}{50\ \text{Hz}} = 15\ \text{s} \]

Frame-rate arithmetic (§2.1–2.2): Mel hop, conv stride, adapter pooling; encoder sliding window in seconds.

Guide

This line is just the frame rate arithmetic. Sixteen thousand samples per second divided by a hop of 160 gives 100 Mel frames per second; the strided convolution halves that to 50; the adapter divides by four to reach 12.5 per second, which is one step every 80 milliseconds. The encoder window of 750 frames at 50 per second covers 15 seconds. Use these numbers when you explain the audio path of a model.

(vi)\[ \operatorname{RMSNorm}(x) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d} x_i^2 + \epsilon}} \odot \gamma \]

Standard definition (Zhang & Sennrich 2019), not written in the paper. γ = learned gain.

Guide

RMS norm is the standard normalisation used throughout the model, written out here because the paper only names it. Each feature is divided by the root mean square of all d features, plus a small epsilon for safety, then scaled by a learned gain gamma. Unlike layer norm it does not subtract the mean. Ada RMS-Norm in equation two simply adds a delay dependent scale on top of this.

(vii)\[ \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}} + \lambda \,\log^2 Z, \qquad Z = \sum_{v} e^{\ell_v} \]

z-loss in its standard form (PaLM); the paper names it but gives neither formula nor λ. Keeps log Z near 0, so logits cannot grow without bound.

Guide

The z loss is added to the usual cross entropy. Z is the softmax normaliser, the sum of the exponentials of all logits, and the penalty lambda times log Z squared pushes log Z toward zero, so logits cannot grow without bound. The paper names this loss but gives neither the formula nor lambda, so this is the standard form from PaLM. It solves the norm drift shown in the problem section.

(viii)\[ \text{WER} = \frac{S + D + I}{N} \]

Word error rate, the metric of every table (standard; not written in the paper). S, D, I = substituted, deleted, inserted words; N = words in the reference. CER is the same over characters (zh, ja).

Guide

Word error rate is the metric in every table, and you will likely use it in your own evaluation. Count the substituted, deleted and inserted words needed to turn the model output into the reference, and divide by the number of reference words. Character error rate does the same over characters, used for Chinese and Japanese. Your score depends heavily on text normalisation, which makes it a useful experiment to run.

§7Putting it into practice

Using Voxtral Realtime in your project

  • Inputs: speech only, output text only. No image and no text prompt, so for a text + image + voice task use it as the speech-to-text stage of a pipeline: transcribe the spoken question, then give transcript + image to a small VLM (e.g. SmolVLM or TinyLLaVA from this atlas) that you fine-tune.
  • Size: one released variant, 4.4B (Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime-2602). About 9 GB of weights in 16-bit, so inference on a free T4 (16 GB) is plausible; QLoRA on the 3.4B decoder may fit, but library support (Transformers / PEFT / bitsandbytes) for this architecture is something to check before you commit.
  • Where LoRA would go (if you fine-tune it): the decoder’s attention and FFN projections, keeping the causal encoder frozen; the paper itself does full training, not LoRA. Note that training data must be in its [P]/[W] frame format, which needs word-level timestamps: much harder than plain (audio, text) pairs. Using it frozen is the simpler route.
  • Delay setting: most fine-tuning tasks are not live, so pick a long delay: FLEURS WER drops from 8.72% at 480 ms to 6.73% at 2400 ms. Streaming only matters if you build a live demo (vLLM serving, §4).
  • Fairness and normalization: Arabic vs English is a ready-made fairness test: 22.53% vs 4.90% WER on FLEURS at 480 ms, and every model is above 45% on Arabic Common Voice. The paper does not describe its text normalizer, so apply one consistently (case, punctuation, diacritics, digits) before computing WER, and report CER where words are not space-separated.
Guide

Use this box to plan your project. Voxtral Realtime only hears speech and writes text, so for a text, image and voice task treat it as the speech to text stage and send its transcript and the image to a small vision language model that you fine tune with QLoRA. It comes in one 4.4 billion parameter size; check library and memory support before trying to fine tune it on a T4, because its training data also needs word timestamps. Choose a long delay for offline work, and use Arabic versus English for your fairness experiment.

An efficient small-model backbone

LFM2 Technical Report

Liquid AI Team (A. Amini, A. Banaszak, H. Benoit, … R. Hasani, M. Lechner, … D. Rus, … N. Tumma) · Liquid AI · arXiv 2511.23404v1, Nov 2025 (published 1 Dec 2025) · open weights at huggingface.co/LiquidAI

LFM2 is a family of small open models built to run fast on phones and laptop CPUs. A search that measured real on-device speed found that a stack of cheap gated short convolutions plus a few grouped-query attention layers is enough; the report then bolts a SigLIP2 image encoder onto this backbone (LFM2-VL) and an audio encoder plus a speech-code decoder (LFM2-Audio), and also derives a retrieval model (LFM2-ColBERT).

Text models
350M · 700M · 1.2B · 2.6B · 8.3B MoE (1.5B active)
Backbone (16-layer sizes)
10 gated conv + 6 GQA
Context · vocab
32,768 tokens · 65,536 BPE
CPU speed
up to ≈2× prefill & decode
LFM2-VL (text + image)
450M · 1.6B · 3B
LFM2-Audio (text + speech)
1.5B · WER 2.03 on LS-clean
Reading guide

The LFM2 report asks how to build small language models that run fast on phones and laptop processors while still being good at real tasks. Its answer is a minimal hybrid backbone: mostly cheap gated short convolutions with only a few attention layers, chosen by measuring speed on the actual devices, plus careful distillation and post-training. On top of that backbone it builds LFM2-VL for images and LFM2-Audio for speech, which is why it matters for multimodal fine-tuning. The tab starts with the big picture of all input paths, then the problems, the method for the backbone and both multimodal variants, every equation and figure, the result tables, and a box on how to put it into practice. In the atlas it is the sixth of eleven papers, after the two Voxtral speech papers and before the omni models, starting with MiniMind-O.

§0Before you read

LFM2 is a report about speed on ordinary hardware: it redesigns the language-model backbone so it runs fast on a phone or laptop CPU, then reuses that backbone for an image model (LFM2-VL) and a speech model (LFM2-Audio). To follow it you need four ideas: what a layer has to remember while it generates, how a small model learns from a bigger teacher, how speech can go in as vectors and come out as codes, and where this family sits among the other papers. For a hands-on project it gives you some of the smallest image and speech models in the atlas, which should fit a free Colab or Kaggle GPU for LoRA, but image and voice live in two separate models.

Terms used in this paper

On-device / edge
Running the model on the user's own phone or laptop instead of a data-centre GPU. Memory and battery are tight, and requests come one at a time (batch size 1).
Prefill, decode, TTFT
Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel; decode then generates one token per step. Time to first token (TTFT) is the wait before the first word appears.
KV cache
The keys and values an attention layer stores for every earlier token so it need not recompute them. It grows linearly with context length and dominates memory on long inputs.
Gated short convolution
LFM2's main layer: two input-dependent gates around a convolution that mixes each position with its two predecessors. Cheap, and it needs only a two-token state while decoding.
GQA (grouped-query attention)
Attention in which several query heads share one key/value head, which shrinks the KV cache. LFM2-1.2B has 32 query heads sharing 8 KV heads.
Knowledge distillation
Training a small student to match a larger teacher's output probabilities. LFM2 keeps only the teacher's Top-32 tokens per position (Top-K distillation).
MoE (mixture of experts)
A layer with many feed-forward "experts" of which a router picks a few per token. LFM2-8B-A1B has 8.3B parameters but uses about 1.5B per token (32 experts, top-4).
llama.cpp Q4_0, ExecuTorch 8da4w
CPU runtimes and their compressed formats used for the speed tests. Q4_0 stores weights in 4 bits with one scale per block of 32; 8da4w means 4-bit weights with 8-bit dynamically quantized activations.
SigLIP2, PixelUnshuffle
SigLIP2 is Google's image encoder that turns image patches into vectors. PixelUnshuffle merges each 2 × 2 group of patch vectors into one, so the language model sees four times fewer image tokens.
Log-mel, FastConformer
A log-mel spectrogram is sound as energy per frequency band over time. FastConformer is an efficient speech encoder (convolution plus attention) that LFM2-Audio uses to turn it into vectors.
Mimi, RVQ codes
Mimi is Kyutai's neural audio codec. Residual vector quantization (RVQ) describes each 80 ms frame with a stack of codes, each correcting what the previous left out; LFM2-Audio predicts 8.
WER
Word error rate: substitutions plus deletions plus insertions, divided by the number of reference words. Lower is better; LFM2-Audio gets 2.03 % on LibriSpeech test-clean.
VoiceBench
A set of 9 speech-in, text-out chatbot tasks (open answers judged by GPT-4o, multiple choice, instruction following, refusals) used to score LFM2-Audio's conversation skills.
MMLU, IFEval, GSM8K
Text benchmarks in the results: MMLU tests knowledge with multiple-choice questions across many subjects, IFEval checks whether instructions such as "answer in 3 bullets" are followed, GSM8K is grade-school maths word problems.
Guide

These fourteen terms are the vocabulary the report assumes. The first group is about speed on a device: prefill, decode, time to first token and the KV cache. The next covers the architecture: gated short convolution, grouped-query attention and mixture of experts. Then the inputs: SigLIP2 and PixelUnshuffle for images, log-mel, FastConformer and Mimi codes for audio. Finally the scores: word error rate, VoiceBench, MMLU, IFEval and GSM8K. Come back here whenever a name in the tables is unfamiliar.

§2Big picture

The backbone is what is new: most layers are a cheap gated short convolution (kernel 3) and only a few are attention. The multimodal models reuse it unchanged and add the usual encoder + connector. For a text + image + voice task you will need two of these models, or one model plus a speech-to-text step.

§3The problem

  • Edge budgets are hard limits. Time-to-first-token, steady decode latency and peak RAM on a phone CPU decide whether a model is usable at all; datacenter-oriented families optimise for large batches instead.
  • Recent hybrids add operators (linear attention, SSMs, long convolutions) whose benefit was measured with proxies such as perplexity or cache size. Liquid AI's earlier STAR search showed these proxies do not transfer to real device latency or task scores.
  • Small models need a teacher, but storing a full 65,536-way distribution per training token is too costly (Problem B).
  • Multimodal inputs are long. A high-resolution image can produce thousands of patch tokens, and a speech codec produces 8 codes per 80 ms frame; both must be squeezed before a 1B-class model can use them on a CPU.

§4Method

4.1 Hardware-in-the-loop architecture search (§2.1)

  1. Objectives: quality (50+ internal evals: knowledge, reasoning, instruction following, multilingual, tool use, math, long context), latency (TTFT, p50/p95 ms per token, prefill tokens/s at batch 1), peak memory (max RSS at 4K and 32K).
  2. Search space: local blocks (gated short conv with varying kernel, sliding-window attention, linear attention, S4, Liquid-S4, S5, RTF, Mamba, Mamba2, CfC), global blocks (GQA with QK-Norm), SwiGLU FFNs, layouts and MoE options.
  3. Profile on device: identical settings, ExecuTorch 8da4w and llama.cpp Q4_0 on Galaxy S24 Ultra and Ryzen HX 370.
  4. Select: discard any candidate over budget, rank the rest by hypervolume improvement on the 3-D Pareto front, carry survivors forward.
Guide

These four steps are the search procedure in order. First define what counts as good: quality, latency and peak memory. Then list every building block the search may use, from sliding-window attention to Mamba. Then compile each candidate with the same quantized runtimes the company ships and time it on the target devices. Finally throw away anything over budget and keep the Pareto survivors. The key lesson is to optimize the real objective, not a proxy like perplexity.

4.2 The LFM2 backbone (§2.2–2.3)

Pseudo-code (written from the §2.2 text; the paper has no Algorithm boxes)
def gated_short_conv(h): # h: [L, d]
  B, C, h_t = split(W_in @ h, 3) # W_in: d → 3d
  y = B * h_t # input-dependent gate
  z = depthwise_conv1d(y, k=3) # mixes positions t-2, t-1, t
  return W_out @ (C * z) # W_out: d → d

def lfm2_layer(x): # pre-norm RMSNorm, residuals
  x = x + SeqBlock(RMSNorm(x)) # SeqBlock = gated_short_conv OR GQA(RoPE, QK-Norm)
  return x + FFN(RMSNorm(x)) # FFN = SwiGLU, or MoE (32 experts, top-4) in LFM2-8B-A1B
Guide

The pseudo-code restates the same block as runnable steps, since the paper gives it only as one line of math. The first function is the gated short convolution; the second is a full layer, with pre-norm, a residual connection around the sequence block, and another around the feedforward block. The sequence block is either the convolution or grouped-query attention. When you add LoRA in your own project, the two linear layers in the first function are natural targets.

Guide

The hyperparameter table tells you the exact layout of each size. The three smallest models have sixteen layers, of which six are attention and ten are convolution blocks; the 2.6 billion model has thirty layers with eight attention. All use eight key-value groups with head size sixty-four and a convolution kernel of three. The mixture-of-experts model has thirty-two experts per layer and activates four per token, which is why only 1.5 billion of its 8.3 billion parameters run per token.

  • Tokenizer: byte-level BPE, 65,536 tokens, trained with focus on English, Japanese, Arabic, Korean, Spanish, French, German, plus JSON/code; special tokens for fill-in-the-middle, tool calling and ChatML.
  • MoE (LFM2-8B-A1B): first two layers dense, all others MoE with 32 SwiGLU experts, top-4 per token, normalised sigmoid router with adaptive routing biases.

4.3 Pre-training with decoupled Top-K distillation (§3)

Data: ≈75 % English, 20 % multilingual, 5 % code (MoE: 60/25/15); 50 % of code uses fill-in-the-middle. Stages: 10T tokens at 4,096 context (MoE: 12T), then 1T higher-quality long-context tokens at 32,768 context. Teacher: an internal LFM1-7B, only its Top-32 logits per token are kept.

4.4 Post-training (§4)

  1. SFT: 5.39M samples from 67 sources (8B-A1B: 9.24M from 79), 80 % English + 20 % across 7 languages; human screen, LLM-judge scoring, refusal and style filtering, exact/near/semantic dedup, decontamination. Curriculum: 12 models answer every item; items are ordered from easy (most models right) to hard. 3 epochs, 32K context, cosine LR 3×10⁻⁵ → 10⁻⁷, AdamW, 8 × H100.
  2. Preference alignment: ≈1M conversations, 5 on-policy samples each scored by an LLM jury; best = chosen, worst = rejected; CLAIR revisions for instruction following; ≈700K pairs; a length-normalised DPO/APO family (Eqs. 3–5).
  3. Model merging: model soup, task arithmetic, TIES, DARE, DELLA tried in parallel; best merge kept (Eqs. 18–23).
Guide

Post-training turns the pretrained model into an assistant in three stages. Supervised fine-tuning uses about five million filtered, deduplicated samples ordered from easy to hard by how many of twelve reference models solve them. Preference alignment samples five answers per prompt, lets an LLM jury pick the best and worst, and trains with a length-normalized loss. Model merging then combines the best candidates. The curriculum idea is simple enough to reuse in your own fine-tuning data.

Epochs2
Guide

These are the settings for the preference-alignment stage. Beta, the KL coefficient that scales the implicit reward in equation five, is five. The learning rate is tiny, peaking at eight times ten to the minus seven with cosine decay, the batch is two thousand and forty-eight, context is one thousand and twenty-four tokens, and training runs for two epochs. Small learning rates like this are typical when you only nudge an already fine-tuned model.

4.5 LFM2-VL: adding vision (§5)

Sizes: LFM2-VL-450M = SigLIP2 Base-86M + LFM2-350M; LFM2-VL-1.6B = SigLIP2 So400M + LFM2-1.2B; LFM2-VL-3B = SigLIP2 So400M + LFM2-2.6B. The NaFlex SigLIP2 keeps native aspect ratio and variable resolution.

4.6 Training the multimodal variants (§5.2, §6.3)

  1. VL stage 1: connector only, captioning pairs, higher LR, 2,048 context.
  2. VL stage 2: all parts, LR ratio 5 : 5 : 1 (backbone : connector : encoder), weight decay 10⁻⁶, 32K packed context, no tiling (up to 4 tiles in OCR runs), ≈50B tokens.
  3. VL stage 3: multimodal SFT with tiling, ≈50B tokens, image share 5–30 % of samples; ≈5 % multi-image, ≈70 % multi-turn; no bounding-box grounding; candidate runs merged linearly.
  4. Audio: alignment (MLP connector on ASR, backbone and encoder frozen) → mid-training on ≈100B tokens (≈62 % text, 25 % audio-output frames, 13 % audio-input embeddings) → post-training. Loss only on discrete targets: text tokens and 8 codebooks.
Guide

The vision model first aligns the connector on captions, then trains everything with the vision encoder at one fifth of the learning rate, then does supervised fine-tuning with tiling on and five to thirty percent image samples. The audio model aligns the connector on speech recognition data, then mid-trains on about one hundred billion tokens. Losses are only on discrete outputs, text tokens and speech codes, never on the continuous audio inputs.

4.7 LFM2-Audio: speech in, speech out (§6)

Input: 16 kHz audio → 128-d log-mel (25 ms window, 10 ms stride) → strided convolutions (8× downsampling) → 17 FastConformer layers (512-d) → MLP to 2048-d. One embedding = 80 ms, 12.5 per second, fed to LFM2-1.2B like text embeddings. Output: continuous input, but discrete output (8-codebook Mimi RVQ codes), so recognition keeps rich features while generation stays cheap.

Pseudo-code: interleaved generation (from §6.2.1)
state = TEXT; text_done = False
while True:
  for _ in range(6 if not text_done else 0): # 6 text tokens
    tok = sample(text_head(backbone_step()))
    if tok == END_OF_TEXT: text_done = True; break
  for _ in range(12 if not text_done else INF): # 12 audio frames (all remaining after text ends)
    e = backbone_step()
    codes = rq_transformer(e, steps=8) # c1..c8, one per codebook
    if END_OF_AUDIO in codes: return
    stream_to_detokenizer(codes); feed_back(sum(embed(c) for c in codes))
Guide

The pseudo-code turns the interleaved schedule into a loop. The model alternates six text tokens with twelve audio frames, and each audio frame is one backbone step plus eight depth-decoder steps whose code embeddings are summed and fed back. When the text ends, the model keeps producing audio until it emits the end-of-audio code. If you ever use LFM2-Audio for spoken answers, this is the loop your library runs for you.

Detokenizer: the Mimi decoder was too slow, so a Vocos-style 35M LFM2 variant (8 layers: 5 gated conv + 3 sliding-window attention, width 512) upsamples frames 6× and predicts log-magnitude and phase of STFT frames; an inverse STFT gives 24 kHz audio. Trained as a GAN (multi-period + multi-resolution discriminators; mel L1 + hinge + feature matching), 16 × 2.4 s clips, 1M steps.

Table 10. LFM2-Audio data per epoch (≈472K hours of audio in + out; for scale, Whisper used ≈680K hours).
Dataset type# Text tokensInput audio (h)Output audio (h)

Guide

The audio data table shows the scale behind LFM2-Audio. Per epoch there are about thirteen billion text tokens, one hundred and forty-six thousand hours of input speech and three hundred and twenty-six thousand hours of output speech, mostly from audio chat instruction tuning. That is about four hundred and seventy-two thousand hours in total, close to Whisper's six hundred and eighty thousand. A few hundred training examples are tiny by comparison, which is exactly why LoRA is the right tool.

4.8 LFM2-ColBERT-350M (§7)

§5Every equation

All 23 numbered equations (main text and Appendices A–B) plus the important unnumbered displays, in paper order. Eqs. 1–2 are one objective split over two lines in the paper.

–\[ (\mathbf{B},\mathbf{C},\tilde{\mathbf{h}})=\operatorname{Linear}(\mathbf{h}),\quad \mathbf{y}=\mathbf{B}\odot\tilde{\mathbf{h}},\quad \mathbf{z}=\operatorname{Conv}_k(\mathbf{y}),\quad \mathbf{o}=\operatorname{Linear}_{\text{out}}(\mathbf{C}\odot\mathbf{z}) \]

§2.2, unnumbered. Gated short convolution block: \(\mathbf{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d}\); Linear maps \(d\to 3d\) and is split into B, C, \(\tilde{\mathbf{h}}\); \(\operatorname{Conv}_k\) is depthwise along the sequence with \(k=3\); \(\odot\) is element-wise product.

Guide

This equation is the gated short convolution written compactly. A linear layer turns the hidden sequence h into three parts, B, C and h tilde. Then y equals B times h tilde element-wise, z is a depthwise convolution of y with kernel size k, and the output o is a linear layer applied to C times z. It is the formula behind the block diagram in the method section.

–\[ P_T(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{T}(x_c)}P_T(x\mid x_c),\qquad P_T(x\mid\mathcal{T},x_c)=\frac{P_T(x\mid x_c)}{P_T(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c)}\quad (x\in\mathcal{T}) \]

§3.3, unnumbered (same for the student \(P_S\)). \(\mathcal{T}(x_c)\) = teacher’s Top-K set (K = 32) for context \(x_c\): its total mass, and the distribution renormalised inside it.

Guide

These definitions prepare the distillation loss. P T of the set T is the total probability the teacher gives to its top-K tokens for a context x c. The second part renormalizes the teacher distribution inside that set so it sums to one. The same definitions hold for the student, P S. Equations one and two are built from these two quantities.

–\[ p^{(\tau)}(x)=\frac{p(x)^{1/\tau}}{\sum_y p(y)^{1/\tau}},\qquad D^{(\tau)}_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\,\Vert\,q)=\tau^2\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(p^{(\tau)}\,\Vert\,q^{(\tau)}\big) \]

§3.3, unnumbered (= Eq. 12). Temperature \(\tau\) flattens a distribution; the \(\tau^2\) keeps gradient size comparable across temperatures.

Guide

This defines temperature. Raising every probability to the power one over tau and renormalizing flattens the distribution when tau is larger than one. The tempered KL divergence is multiplied by tau squared so the gradient size stays comparable across temperatures. The paper applies this only inside the top-K set, which is the whole point of the decoupled method.

(1)\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{DTK}}(x_c)=\underbrace{D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\operatorname{Bern}(P_T(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c))\,\Vert\,\operatorname{Bern}(P_S(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c))\big)}_{\mathcal{L}_B} \]

Binary (Bernoulli) KL: the student must put the same total probability inside the teacher’s Top-K set as the teacher. Untempered.

Guide

Equation one is the first half of the distillation loss, L B. It is a KL divergence between two coin flips: the teacher's probability that the next token falls in its top-K set, and the student's probability of the same event. It teaches the student how much mass belongs in the top set, and it is left untempered.

(2)\[ \;+\;\underbrace{P_T(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c)\,D^{(\tau)}_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(P_T(\cdot\mid\mathcal{T},x_c)\,\Vert\,P_S(\cdot\mid\mathcal{T},x_c)\big)}_{\mathcal{L}_T} \]

Conditional Top-K KL, weighted by the teacher’s Top-K mass: matches the relative probabilities inside the set; temperature is applied only here. Total loss = \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{DTK}}\) + next-token cross-entropy.

Guide

Equation two is the second half, L T. It compares teacher and student inside the top-K set after renormalizing both, with temperature applied, and weights the result by the teacher's top-K mass. It teaches the relative ranking of the likely tokens. Together with equation one it forms the decoupled Top-K objective, which is then added to ordinary cross-entropy on the true next token.

–\[ p_i=\frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^{J} r_{ij},\qquad r_{ij}\in\{0,1\},\; J=12 \]

§4.2.1, unnumbered. Curriculum difficulty: share of 12 reference models that answer item \(x_i\) correctly; high \(p_i\) = easy, trained first.

Guide

This short formula defines difficulty for the curriculum. For item i, r i j is one if model j answered correctly and zero otherwise, and p i is the average over twelve models. A high p i means an easy item. The training set is sorted from easy to hard using a predictor of p i, a trick you could copy when ordering your own fine-tuning examples.

(3)\[ \mathcal{L}(\pi_\theta;\pi_{\text{ref}})=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_w,y_l)\sim\mathcal{D}}\big[\omega\cdot f\big(\Delta(x,y_w,y_l)-m\big)+\lambda\cdot g\big(\delta(x,y_w,y_l)\big)\big] \]

General length-normalised preference loss over prompt \(x\), chosen \(y_w\), rejected \(y_l\): a relative term (weight \(\omega\), margin \(m\)) and an absolute term (weight \(\lambda\)).

Guide

Equation three is a general recipe for preference training. Given a prompt x, a chosen answer y w and a rejected answer y l, it combines a relative term, how much more the model prefers the chosen answer minus a margin m, weighted by omega, with an absolute term weighted by lambda. The functions f and g pick the exact variant, as the special cases below show.

(4)\[ \Delta(x,y_w,y_l)=\frac{r_\theta(x,y_w)}{|y_w|}-\frac{r_\theta(x,y_l)}{|y_l|},\qquad \delta(x,y_w,y_l)=\sigma\!\Big(\frac{r_\theta(x,y_w)}{|y_w|}\Big)-\sigma\!\Big(\frac{r_\theta(x,y_l)}{|y_l|}\Big) \]

Rewards are divided by response length \(|y|\) (token count) so the model is not rewarded for longer answers; \(\sigma\) = sigmoid.

Guide

Equation four defines the two ingredients of the preference loss. Delta is the difference between the chosen and rejected rewards, each divided by its answer length in tokens. Small delta is the difference of their sigmoids. Dividing by length stops the model from learning that longer answers are automatically better.

(5)\[ r_\theta(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)} \]

Implicit reward: log-ratio of the trained policy to the frozen reference (SFT) model, scaled by the KL coefficient \(\beta\) (= 5.0, Table 5).

Guide

Equation five is the implicit reward used in direct preference optimization. It is beta times the log ratio between the probability the trained policy gives an answer and the probability the frozen reference model gives it. Beta is five here, from Table 5. A positive reward means the model now likes that answer more than before training.

–\[ \text{DPO: }\{\omega{=}1,\,f(x){=}\log\sigma(x),\,m{=}0,\,\lambda{=}0\}\quad \text{APO-zero: }\{\omega{=}0,\,\lambda{=}1,\,g(x){=}x\}\quad \text{joint: }\{\omega{=}1,\,f{=}\log\sigma,\,m{=}0.1,\,\lambda{=}0.2,\,g(x){=}x\} \]

§4.3.2, special cases of Eq. 3 (length-normalised). The margin \(m\) makes the relative term SimPO-like; the absolute term anchors probabilities.

Guide

These settings show that equation three contains known methods as special cases. With omega one, f equal to log sigmoid and no absolute term you get length-normalized DPO. With only the absolute term you get APO-zero. The paper also mixes both with a margin of zero point one and lambda of zero point two, which behaves like SimPO plus an anchor on probabilities.

–\[ L=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\log\frac{\exp(l_{n,y_n})}{\sum_{i=1}^{V}\exp(l_{n,i})} \]

§6.3, unnumbered. Token-level cross-entropy, computed separately for the text vocabulary (\(L_T\)) and each of the 8 Mimi codebooks (\(L_1,\dots,L_8\)); no loss on continuous audio inputs.

Guide

This is the ordinary cross-entropy loss that LFM2-Audio is trained with. For each of N target tokens it takes the log of the softmax probability of the correct token y n among V choices, and averages with a minus sign. It is computed separately for text tokens and for each of the eight speech codebooks, and never for the continuous audio inputs.

–\[ \mathcal{L}_A=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{8}w_k L_k}{\sum_{k=1}^{8}w_k},\quad w_1=100,\; w_8=1,\; w_k=100^{(8-k)/7}\ (\text{our reading});\qquad \mathcal{L}=\frac{N_T L_T+N_A \mathcal{L}_A}{N_T+N_A} \]

§6.3, stated only in words: codebook weights decay exponentially from 100 to 1 (the exact formula is our reconstruction), and text and audio losses are averaged weighted by their token counts \(N_T, N_A\).

Guide

This formula writes down what the paper says only in words, so treat the exact weights as our reconstruction. The eight codebook losses are averaged with weights that decay exponentially from one hundred for the first, semantic codebook to one for the last. The total loss then averages text and audio losses weighted by how many tokens of each are in the batch. Emphasizing the first codebooks improved perceived audio quality.

–\[ \frac{16\,000\ \text{samples/s}}{160\ \text{(10 ms hop)}\times 8}=12.5\ \text{audio embeddings per second}\;\Rightarrow\;80\ \text{ms each} \]

§6.1.1, arithmetic from the stated numbers. One Mimi output frame (8 codes) also covers 80 ms, so input and output run at the same rate.

Guide

This arithmetic explains the audio rate. Sixteen thousand samples per second with a ten millisecond hop give one hundred log-mel frames per second, and the encoder downsamples by eight, so there are twelve and a half embeddings per second, each covering eighty milliseconds. A ten-second spoken question therefore becomes only about one hundred and twenty-five tokens for the language model.

(6)\[ \operatorname{ColBERT}(x)=\operatorname{Linear}\big(\text{LFM2-Transformer}(x)\big) \]

Token embeddings from the LFM2-350M backbone projected 1024 → 128 without bias; \(x\) is a query or a document.

Guide

Equation six defines the retrieval encoder. Text, either a query or a document, goes through the LFM2 backbone, and a linear layer without bias projects each token vector from one thousand and twenty-four down to one hundred and twenty-eight dimensions. Smaller vectors make the index cheaper to store and compare.

(7)\[ S(q,d)=\sum_i\max_j\ \operatorname{sim}(q_i,d_j) \]

MaxSim late interaction: for every query token take the most similar document token (cosine) and sum.

Guide

Equation seven is the MaxSim score. For every query token i, find the document token j with the highest cosine similarity, then sum these best matches over all query tokens. It lets each word of the question find its own evidence in the document, as in the diagram of the method section.

(8)\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{distill}}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\big(s_i^T-S(q,d_i)\big)^2 \]

MSE between min-max-normalised cross-encoder teacher scores \(s_i^T\) and the student’s MaxSim scores over \(m=8\) documents per query. (The paper refers to MaxSim as "Equation 2"; it is Eq. 7.)

Guide

Equation eight trains the retriever by imitation. For a query with eight documents, a strong cross-encoder teacher gives relevance scores s i T, and the loss is the mean squared difference between those and the student's MaxSim scores. The paper says the score is equation two, but it means equation seven.

(9)\[ D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(P_T(\cdot\mid x_c)\,\Vert\,P_S(\cdot\mid x_c)\big)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{A}}P_T(x\mid x_c)\log\frac{P_T(x\mid x_c)}{P_S(x\mid x_c)} \]

Appendix A.1. Full forward KL over the whole vocabulary \(\mathcal{A}\) (65,536 tokens): what we would like but cannot compute from Top-K logits.

Guide

Equation nine is the full forward KL divergence between teacher and student over the whole vocabulary A, the sum of teacher probability times the log ratio. It is what ideal distillation would minimize, but it needs all sixty-five thousand teacher probabilities per token, which LFM2 does not store.

(10)\[ \begin{aligned}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(P_T(\cdot\mid x_c)\Vert P_S(\cdot\mid x_c)\big)&=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\operatorname{Bern}(P_T(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c))\Vert\operatorname{Bern}(P_S(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c))\big)\\&\quad+P_T(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c)\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(P_T(\cdot\mid\mathcal{T},x_c)\Vert P_S(\cdot\mid\mathcal{T},x_c)\big)\\&\quad+P_T(\bar{\mathcal{T}}\mid x_c)\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(P_T(\cdot\mid\bar{\mathcal{T}},x_c)\Vert P_S(\cdot\mid\bar{\mathcal{T}},x_c)\big)\end{aligned} \]

Chain rule: exact split into membership term + inside-Top-K term + tail term (\(\bar{\mathcal{T}}=\mathcal{A}\setminus\mathcal{T}\)).

Guide

Equation ten splits that full KL exactly into three parts using the chain rule: a coin-flip term for being inside or outside the top-K set, a KL inside the set weighted by its mass, and a KL over the tail, T bar, weighted by the tail mass. Only the first two can be computed from stored top-K logits.

(11)\[ \mathcal{L}^{LB}_{\text{DTK}}(x_c)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\operatorname{Bern}(P_T(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c))\Vert\operatorname{Bern}(P_S(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c))\big)+P_T(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c)\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(P_T(\cdot\mid\mathcal{T},x_c)\Vert P_S(\cdot\mid\mathcal{T},x_c)\big) \]

Drop the non-negative tail term (teacher tail logits are unavailable): a lower bound on Eq. 9, untempered.

Guide

Equation eleven simply drops the tail term from equation ten. Because a KL divergence is never negative, what remains is a lower bound on the full KL. It is still untempered here; the next two equations add temperature in the safe place.

(12)\[ p^{(\tau)}(x)=\frac{p(x)^{1/\tau}}{\sum_y p(y)^{1/\tau}},\qquad D^{(\tau)}_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q)=\tau^2 D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(p^{(\tau)}\Vert q^{(\tau)}\big),\quad \tau\ge 1 \]

Temperature definition, applied only to the two conditional (inside-Top-K) distributions.

Guide

Equation twelve repeats the temperature definition from the main text, now for tau of at least one. It is applied only to the two conditional distributions inside the top-K set, never to the membership coin flip or to the weight in front.

(13)\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{DTK}}(x_c)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\operatorname{Bern}(P_T(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c))\Vert\operatorname{Bern}(P_S(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c))\big)+P_T(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c)\,D^{(\tau)}_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(P_T(\cdot\mid\mathcal{T},x_c)\Vert P_S(\cdot\mid\mathcal{T},x_c)\big) \]

The boxed final objective (= Eqs. 1 + 2): \(\mathcal{L}_B\) matches the amount of mass on the Top-K, \(\mathcal{L}_T\) matches its shape.

Guide

Equation thirteen is the final decoupled Top-K objective, boxed in the paper and identical to equations one and two. The first term matches how much mass is on the top-K set; the second, tempered term matches the shape inside it. This is the distillation loss actually used in LFM2 pre-training.

(14)\[ \lim_{\tau\to\infty}P_S^{(\tau)}(x)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\ \ (\forall x\in\mathcal{A}),\qquad \lim_{\tau\to\infty}\hat{P}_T^{(\tau)}(x)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}, & x\in\mathcal{T}\\ 0, & x\notin\mathcal{T}\end{cases} \]

Why naive truncation + temperature fails: the tempered student becomes uniform over all tokens while the truncated teacher is uniform only over the Top-K, so \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\to\log(|\mathcal{A}|/|\mathcal{T}|)\) and \(D^{(\tau)}_{\mathrm{KL}}\) grows like \(\tau^2\).

Guide

Equation fourteen proves why the naive approach is unstable. As temperature grows, the tempered student becomes uniform over all tokens, while the truncated teacher becomes uniform over only the top-K. Their KL approaches the log of vocabulary size over K, and after multiplying by tau squared the loss keeps growing. Conditioning both on the top-K set removes this mismatch.

(15)\[ \begin{aligned}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(P_S(\cdot\mid x_c)\Vert P_T(\cdot\mid x_c)\big)&=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\operatorname{Bern}(P_S(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c))\Vert\operatorname{Bern}(P_T(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c))\big)\\&\quad+P_S(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c)\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(P_S(\cdot\mid\mathcal{T},x_c)\Vert P_T(\cdot\mid\mathcal{T},x_c)\big)\\&\quad+P_S(\bar{\mathcal{T}}\mid x_c)\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(P_S(\cdot\mid\bar{\mathcal{T}},x_c)\Vert P_T(\cdot\mid\bar{\mathcal{T}},x_c)\big)\end{aligned} \]

Appendix A.2. The same chain-rule split for the reverse KL (student first), with \(Z=\mathbf{1}[x\in\mathcal{T}(x_c)]\).

Guide

Equation fifteen is the same chain-rule split, but for the reverse KL, where the student comes first. It again produces a membership term, a term inside the top-K set and a tail term, now weighted by the student's own masses. The appendix includes it for completeness; LFM2 uses the forward version.

(16)\[ \mathcal{L}^{(LB)}_{\text{rev}}(x_c)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\operatorname{Bern}(P_S(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c))\Vert\operatorname{Bern}(P_T(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c))\big)+P_S(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c)\,D^{(\tau)}_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(P_S(\cdot\mid\mathcal{T},x_c)\Vert P_T(\cdot\mid\mathcal{T},x_c)\big) \]

Computable reverse-KL lower bound (tail dropped), temperature only inside the conditional term.

Guide

Equation sixteen is the computable lower bound for the reverse KL: drop the tail term and put temperature only inside the top-K term. Its weakness is that the student could lower its own top-K mass to shrink the second term, which motivates the next equation.

(17)\[ \mathcal{L}^{(tw)}_{\text{rev}}(x_c)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\operatorname{Bern}(P_S(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c))\Vert\operatorname{Bern}(P_T(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c))\big)+P_T(\mathcal{T}\mid x_c)\,D^{(\tau)}_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(P_S(\cdot\mid\mathcal{T},x_c)\Vert P_T(\cdot\mid\mathcal{T},x_c)\big) \]

Teacher-weighted surrogate: weighting by the teacher mass removes the student’s incentive to shrink \(P_S(\mathcal{T})\); no longer a strict bound.

Guide

Equation seventeen fixes that incentive by weighting the inside-the-set term with the teacher's mass instead of the student's. It is no longer a strict bound, but in practice it stops the student from shrinking its top-K mass. Like the others, only the conditional term is tempered.

(18)\[ \theta_{\text{merged}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i\theta_i,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i=1 \]

Appendix B. Model soup: weighted average of \(n\) fine-tuned checkpoints, tensor by tensor.

Guide

Equation eighteen is the simplest way to merge models, a model soup. The merged weights are a weighted average of several fine-tuned checkpoints, with weights summing to one, done tensor by tensor. It needs no extra training, which is why LFM2 tries several merges and keeps the best.

(19)\[ \theta_{\text{merged}}=\theta_0+\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i\tau_i,\qquad \tau_i=\theta_i-\theta_0 \]

Task arithmetic: add weighted task vectors (fine-tuned minus base \(\theta_0\)). Here \(\tau_i\) is a task vector, not a temperature.

Guide

Equation nineteen is task arithmetic. Each fine-tuned model is turned into a task vector, its weights minus the base weights, and the merge adds a weighted sum of task vectors to the base. Note that tau here means a task vector, not a temperature. A LoRA adapter is essentially a compact task vector of this kind.

(20)\[ \theta_{\text{merged}}=\theta_0+\sum_j\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i\tilde{\tau}_{ij}M_{ij}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_iM_{ij}},\qquad \gamma_j=\operatorname{sign}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{\tau}_{ij}\Big),\quad M_{ij}=\mathbf{1}[\operatorname{sign}(\tilde{\tau}_{ij})=\gamma_j] \]

TIES: keep the top-k % magnitudes of each task vector (\(\tilde{\tau}\)), elect a majority sign \(\gamma_j\) per parameter \(j\), average only agreeing entries (the \(\sum_j\) means "for every parameter position").

Guide

Equation twenty is TIES merging. Each task vector is trimmed to its largest entries, a majority sign is elected for every parameter, and only the entries that agree with that sign are averaged. This reduces interference when two fine-tunes push the same weight in opposite directions.

(21)\[ m_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p),\qquad \tilde{\tau}_i=(1-m_i)\odot\tau_i,\qquad \hat{\tau}_i=\frac{\tilde{\tau}_i}{1-p} \]

DARE: randomly drop entries of a task vector with rate \(p\) and rescale the survivors so the expected update is unchanged.

Guide

Equation twenty-one is DARE. Each entry of a task vector is dropped at random with probability p, and the survivors are divided by one minus p so the expected update stays the same. Surprisingly many entries can be dropped without hurting the merged model.

(22)\[ r_i=\operatorname{rank}(|\tau_{ij}|),\qquad p_i=p_{\min}+\frac{\epsilon}{n}\cdot r_i,\qquad p_{\min}=p-\epsilon/2 \]

DELLA: drop probability depends on magnitude rank, so small entries are dropped more often; the average rate stays \(p\), \(\epsilon\) sets the spread.

Guide

Equation twenty-two is the first half of DELLA. Instead of dropping entries uniformly, each gets a drop probability based on its magnitude rank, so small entries are dropped more often. P min is set so that the average drop rate is still p, and epsilon controls how spread out the probabilities are.

(23)\[ m_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_i),\qquad \hat{\tau}_i=\frac{(1-m_i)\odot\tau_i}{1-p_i} \]

DELLA drop and per-entry rescale; combined with TIES sign election and disjoint merge.

Guide

Equation twenty-three completes DELLA: drop each entry with its own probability p i and rescale survivors by one over one minus p i. LFM2 combines this with the TIES sign election. Together, equations eighteen to twenty-three are the menu of merging tricks behind the final checkpoints.

§8Putting it into practice

LFM2 → your project (text + image + voice)

  • What each model accepts natively. No single model in this report takes all three inputs. LFM2 = text only; LFM2-VL = text + one or more images (no audio); LFM2-Audio-1.5B = text + speech in, text or speech out (no images); none takes video. For a task such as "spoken question about a photo", build a pipeline: speech → text with an ASR model (LFM2-Audio-1.5B in sequential/ASR mode, or Whisper) → LFM2-VL with the image and the transcript. Document clearly which part of the pipeline handles which input.
  • Size versus a free T4 (16 GB). Smallest vision model: LFM2-VL-450M (SigLIP2 Base-86M + LFM2-350M), then LFM2-VL-1.6B. Both should fit comfortably with QLoRA (4-bit backbone); the 3B probably fits too, but check peak memory, because one tiled image can add ≈2,800 tokens. LFM2-Audio-1.5B (1.2B backbone + encoder + 115M RQ-Transformer): check. The T4 has no bf16, so train in fp16. The paper trains on H100s and reports no LoRA/QLoRA runs, so these are estimates, not paper results.
  • Where to put LoRA. On the backbone linear layers: q/k/v/output projections of the few GQA layers, the input Linear (d → 3d, which produces B, C, h̃) and the output Linear of every gated conv block, and the SwiGLU FFN linears. Optionally adapt or fully train the small connector MLP. Keep SigLIP2 and the audio encoder frozen: the paper aligns only the connector first and gives the vision encoder the smallest learning rate (5 : 5 : 1). The 3-tap depthwise conv has very few weights; leave it. Print the model to get the exact module names before setting target_modules.
  • What the paper suggests for mixing modalities. Keep some text-only examples in your fine-tuning mix (LFM2-VL kept 30 % text in mid-training and used 5–30 % image samples in SFT) so the model does not lose language skills. You can lower the image-token budget (fewer tiles, smaller images) to save memory, but Fig. 6 shows document/OCR tasks lose far more accuracy than general photo questions.
  • Fairness and normalization angle. The authors state that LFM2-Audio training is dominated by English and other high-resource languages and is likely less robust to low-resource languages and accents; LFM2-VL-3B also varies by language (Table 16: Arabic 73.2 vs German 78.2). So compare Arabic vs English questions, or two speaker groups, through your whole pipeline. ASR errors add to VLM errors, so report WER per group as well as final accuracy. For WER and exact match, normalise references and outputs the same way (case, punctuation, Arabic diacritics, digits vs number words), and report scores with and without it.
Guide

First, note that LFM2-VL handles text and images and LFM2-Audio handles text and speech, so your text plus image plus voice task needs a speech-to-text step before the vision model. Second, start with the 450 million or 1.6 billion vision model under QLoRA on the T4, in fp16. Third, put LoRA on the backbone linear layers and keep the encoders frozen. Finally, plan a language or speaker-group comparison and a normalization ablation.

Omni: text, image and voice together

MiniMind-O Technical Report: An Open Small-Scale Speech-Native Omni Model

Jingyao Gong · Independent researcher · arXiv 2605.03937v1, May 2026 · code github.com/jingyaogong/minimind-o

MiniMind-O is a fully open omni model with only about 0.1B active parameters: it hears speech, sees images, reads text, and answers in text and streaming speech. Frozen SenseVoice (speech) and SigLIP2 (image) encoders feed small MLP projectors into the MiniMind language model (the Thinker); a separate four-layer Talker reads a middle Thinker layer and predicts eight Mimi codec streams that decode to a 24 kHz waveform. The paper shows which design choices matter at this tiny scale: the bridge layer, the Talker width, and low-rank codebook adapters.

Active size
Dense 115M · MoE 317M (A115M)
Inputs → outputs
text, speech, image → text + speech
Frozen parts
SenseVoice 234M · SigLIP2 94.6M · Mimi 96.2M
Talker CER (768-d)
0.0897 dense · 0.0900 MoE
Voice-clone similarity
0.5995 dense · 0.5937 MoE
Training compute
4× RTX 3090, under 4 h per cycle
Reading guide

MiniMind-O asks whether a complete omni model, one that listens, sees, reads and talks back, can work and stay fully open at only about 0.1 billion active parameters. The answer is yes: frozen SenseVoice and SigLIP2 encoders feed small projectors into the MiniMind language model, called the Thinker, and a separate four-layer Talker reads a middle Thinker layer and predicts eight Mimi codec streams that become streaming speech. The paper also shows which choices matter at this scale: the bridge layer, the Talker width, and low-rank codebook adapters. The tab runs from big picture and problem through method, equations and figures to results and a box on putting it into practice. Among the eleven papers it opens the omni group, after LFM2 and before Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni, MiniCPM-o 4.5 and Gemma 4, and it is the smallest model here that takes text, images and voice natively.

§0Before you read

MiniMind-O is the smallest model in the atlas that does the whole loop: it hears speech, sees images, reads text and talks back, with only about 0.1 billion trainable parameters. To follow it you need three ideas: how sound and pictures become tokens a language model can read, how a separate Talker turns the model's hidden states back into audio codes, and how speech output is scored by transcribing it (CER). Code, weights and training data are all open and it trains on consumer GPUs, so it is the most hackable starting point for a text, image and voice project.

Terms used in this paper

Omni model
One model that accepts several input types (here text, speech and images) and can answer in more than one output type (here text and speech).
Thinker and Talker
The Thinker is the language model that understands the input and writes the text answer. The Talker is a smaller second network that reads the Thinker's hidden states and generates speech codes.
SenseVoice-Small
An open speech encoder (234M parameters, frozen here) that turns 16 kHz audio into a sequence of 512-dimensional feature frames.
SigLIP2
An open image encoder, a vision transformer (ViT). The base patch-32 version used here turns a 256-pixel image into 64 tokens of 768 dimensions; it stays frozen.
Projector
A small trainable MLP (LayerNorm, Linear, GELU, Linear) that maps encoder features into the language model's 768-dimensional embedding space.
Placeholder tokens
Special tokens such as <|audio_pad|> and <|image_pad|> reserved in the text sequence; their embeddings are overwritten by projected speech or image features.
Mimi codec and codebooks
A neural audio codec that turns speech into discrete tokens: 12.5 frames per second, each frame described by 8 codes from 8 codebooks of 2,048 entries. Its decoder turns codes back into 24 kHz audio.
Streaming and latency
Streaming means output is played while it is still being generated. Latency is the delay before the first text or the first sound appears.
VAD and barge-in
A voice activity detector (VAD) notices when someone is speaking. Barge-in means the user interrupts; the demo then stops talking and starts a new reply.
CAM++ speaker embedding
A 192-number vector that summarises what a voice sounds like. MiniMind-O uses it, together with reference audio codes, to imitate a chosen voice (voice cloning).
CER and WER
Character and word error rate: substitutions, deletions and insertions needed to turn a transcript into the reference, divided by the reference length. Here the Talker's speech is transcribed and compared with the Thinker's text; lower is better.
T2A, I2T, A2A
The paper's training tasks and datasets: text to audio (speak an answer), image to text, and audio to audio (spoken question, spoken answer).
Dense and MoE
A dense model uses every weight for every token (115M here). A mixture-of-experts (MoE) model has many expert blocks but runs only a few per token: 317M in total, about 115M active.
RTX 3090
A consumer NVIDIA GPU with 24 GB of memory. All training ran on four of them, each training cycle in under four hours; a free Colab T4 has 16 GB.
Guide

These fourteen terms are the vocabulary of this paper. Three matter most. The Thinker is the language model that writes text, and the Talker turns its hidden states into speech. Mimi codes are the discrete audio tokens the Talker predicts, eight per frame. CER, the character error rate, measures how well the spoken answer matches the text answer after transcription, and you can reuse it as a metric in your own evaluation.

§2Big picture

The whole loop (listen, see, think, speak) runs on a backbone of about 64M parameters, so every interface has to be small and measurable. That is exactly what makes it a good object to study and fine-tune on a free GPU.

§3The problem

  • Small models leave no slack: a wrong bridge layer or a Talker narrower than 768 breaks Thinker–Talker consistency (Table 2).
  • Omni systems are hard to reproduce when the sequence layout and codec targets are private; here data and code are released together.

§4Method

  1. Encode. Speech becomes SenseVoice frontend features and runs through the frozen SenseVoice-Small encoder (512-d). Images run through frozen SigLIP2 base/32 at 256 px (64 tokens, 768-d).
  2. Project. A two-layer MLP (LayerNorm, Linear, GELU, Linear) maps each frame to the 768-d MiniMind space, keeping the sequence length.
  3. Inject. The projected frames overwrite the contiguous <|audio_pad|> or <|image_pad|> embeddings in the text sequence; text tokens use the normal embedding table.
  4. Think. The 8-layer MiniMind Thinker (GQA, RoPE, RMSNorm, dense or MoE FFN) predicts the text answer token by token.
  5. Bridge. The hidden state after layer 3 goes through embed_proj, times a learned text scale, and is added to the projected audio-code history, times a learned audio scale.
  6. Speak. The 4-block Talker predicts eight Mimi codebooks with a one-step stagger per layer, through a shared head plus per-codebook low-rank adapters. A voice prompt sits in the same audio buffer.
  7. Stream. As soon as a full eight-code frame exists, the frozen Mimi decoder emits 24 kHz audio, so playback starts before the text is finished.
Guide

The method is a pipeline of seven moves: encode, project, inject, think, bridge, speak and stream. Perception is delegated to frozen encoders, and only a thin MLP translates their frames into MiniMind's space, where they simply overwrite placeholder tokens. The Thinker then writes text, while the Talker reads a middle layer plus its own audio history and emits staggered codes that Mimi turns into sound. For fine-tuning, steps two, four and five are where trainable weights live.

Training schedule actually run (from §5)

train_sft_omni.py # modes: all | audio_proj | vision_proj hardware: 4 × RTX 3090 (24 GB), DDP, bf16, AdamW, batch 32 / GPU, clip 1.0 for variant in [minimind-3o (dense), minimind-3o-moe]: 1. mode=all data=sft_t2a lr=5e-6 epochs=1 # ≈45 min, text → speech 2. mode=audio_proj data=sft_a2a lr=5e-4 epochs=1 # ≈25 min, projector only 3. mode=all data=sft_a2a lr=5e-5 epochs=3 # ≈75 min, speech → speech 4. mode=vision_proj data=sft_i2t lr=5e-5 epochs=1 # ≈45 min, projector only 5. mode=all data=sft_i2t lr=5e-6 epochs=1 # ≈45 min, 768-token context SenseVoice, SigLIP2 and Mimi stay frozen in every pass # note: the paper lists passes by lr/epochs; the exact run order in train.sh # is "full passes over t2a, i2t, a2a, then a projector-only i2t pass"
Guide

The whole training recipe is one script with three modes: all updates Thinker, Talker and projectors, while audio proj and vision proj train only one projector. The passes cover text-to-speech, audio projector alignment, three epochs of speech-to-speech, and image alignment and tuning, with small learning rates for full passes and larger ones for projector-only passes. No pass takes more than about seventy-five minutes on four RTX 3090 cards.

§5Every equation

(1)\[ \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{text}} + \lambda_{\text{audio}} \sum_{q=1}^{8} \mathcal{L}^{(q)}_{\text{audio}} \]

Joint next-token objective for a response with text tokens \(y_{1:T}\) and Mimi codes \(\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{N}^{8\times T'}\): text loss plus a weighted sum of the eight codebook losses; q indexes the codec layer; padding and conditioning positions are masked. The paper does not give the value of \(\lambda_{\text{audio}}\).

Guide

Equation one is the single training objective. L is the total loss, L text is the cross-entropy on the Thinker's response tokens, and the sum adds the eight audio losses, one per Mimi codebook layer q, weighted by lambda audio. Padding, reference codes and the speaker slot are masked, so only real targets count. The paper does not report the value of lambda, so treat it as a setting to find in the code.

(u1)\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{text}} = -\sum_{t} \log p_\theta\!\left(y_t \mid y_{\lt t}, \text{context}\right),\qquad \mathcal{L}^{(q)}_{\text{audio}} = -\sum_{t\,\in\,\text{target}} \log p_\theta\!\left(a_{q,t} \mid \mathbf{a}_{\lt t}, h^{(3)}\right) \]

Unnumbered, implied by the text: both terms are ordinary cross-entropies. Only Thinker response tokens and target Mimi positions count; reference codes and the speaker slot are context, not targets.

Guide

These are the two ingredients of equation one written out. The text loss is minus the log probability of each response token y t given the earlier tokens and the multimodal context. Each audio loss is minus the log probability of code a q t, given earlier codes and the layer-three bridge state h three, summed only over target positions. The paper implies these standard forms rather than printing them.

(u2)\[ \ell_{\text{bridge}} = \left\lfloor \tfrac{L}{2} \right\rfloor - 1 = \left\lfloor \tfrac{8}{2} \right\rfloor - 1 = 3 \]

Unnumbered (code default num_hidden_layers // 2 - 1): with L = 8 Thinker layers the bridge state is taken after layer 3.

Guide

This one line fixes where the Talker listens. L is the number of Thinker layers; the bridge index is L divided by two, rounded down, minus one. With eight layers that gives layer three. It is the code default num hidden layers integer-divided by two minus one, the same middle-layer idea as the Qwen-Omni Thinker and Talker, and the choice that Figure 2 in the problem section motivates.

(u3)\[ x_t = s_{\text{text}}\cdot \operatorname{embed\_proj}\!\big(h^{(3)}_t\big) + s_{\text{audio}}\cdot \operatorname{codec\_proj}\!\big(e_t\big) \]

Unnumbered (§3): the Talker input is the sum of the projected bridge state and the projected audio-code embedding, each multiplied by a learned scalar scale.

Guide

The Talker input at each position is a weighted sum of two streams. x t is the Talker input, h three t is the Thinker's layer-three state passed through embed proj, e t is the audio-code embedding passed through codec proj, and s text and s audio are learned scalar scales. The scales let the model balance meaning from the Thinker against its own audio history. This is the plus node in the middle of Figure 2.

(u4)\[ e_t = \frac{1}{8}\sum_{q=0}^{7}\Big( E\,[a_{q,t}] + B^{\text{emb}}_q\, A^{\text{emb}}_q[a_{q,t}] \Big),\qquad E\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d},\; A^{\text{emb}}_q\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times r},\; B^{\text{emb}}_q\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} \]

Unnumbered, read from Fig. 2: TalkerEmbedding looks up each of the eight codes in one shared table plus a rank-r codebook adapter, then averages over codebooks (the Σ/8 node). V = 2,112 audio vocabulary, d = 768, r = 256 by default. The factor shapes are our reading of the figure.

Guide

This is the low-rank audio embedding. For each of the eight codes at time t, the model looks up the shared table E and adds a small rank r adapter, A for codebook q followed by B for codebook q, then averages over the eight codebooks. V is the audio vocabulary of 2,112, d is 768 and r is 256 by default. The exact factor shapes are read from Figure 2, so treat them as an interpretation.

(u5)\[ \text{logits}_q = W\,z_t + B^{\text{head}}_q A^{\text{head}}_q\, z_t,\qquad W\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d},\; A^{\text{head}}_q\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d},\; B^{\text{head}}_q\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times r} \]

Unnumbered, read from Fig. 2: TalkerHead is one shared linear head plus a d → r → V adapter per codebook applied to the Talker output z. Fig. 8 shows the head rank matters more than the embedding rank.

Guide

This is the low-rank output head, the mirror image of the embedding. The Talker output z t goes through one shared matrix W for all codebooks, plus a codebook-specific path that squeezes d down to rank r with A and back up to the vocabulary V with B. Figure 8 shows this head rank matters more than the embedding rank, because the head must separate eight full distributions over the audio vocabulary.

(u6)\[ \text{start}(q) = t_{\text{assistant}} + q + 1,\qquad q = 0,\dots,7 \]

Unnumbered (§4): the delay pattern. Codebook layer q receives its first target one step after layer q − 1, so a full frame is ready after eight steps.

Guide

The delay pattern in one line. t assistant is the position where the reply starts, and codebook layer q, counted from zero to seven, gets its first target at that position plus q plus one. So the coarse codebook leads and each finer one follows a step later. It explains the diagonal in Figure 3 and the seven-step wait before the first audio in Figure 9.

(u7)\[ e_{t_{\text{spk}}} \leftarrow \operatorname{spk\_proj}(c),\qquad c\in\mathbb{R}^{192}\ \text{(CAM++)} \]

Unnumbered (§3): at the reserved <|audio_spk|> position the Talker embedding is replaced by the projected 192-d CAM++ speaker vector.

Guide

Voice cloning happens by overwriting one embedding. c is the precomputed 192-dimensional CAM++ speaker vector; spk proj maps it to 768 dimensions and it replaces the Talker embedding at the reserved speaker position. Together with right-aligned reference codes, this is the whole speaker mechanism, with no extra encoder at inference, and it is what Table 3 and Table 7 evaluate.

(u8)\[ \text{CER} = \frac{S + D + I}{N_{\text{chars}}}\ \ \text{(ASR transcript of Talker audio vs. Thinker text)} \]

Unnumbered, standard definition used by the evaluation: substitutions, deletions and insertions over reference length; WER is the same on words. Values above 1 are possible (e.g. 1.41 in Table 9).

Guide

CER is the character error rate, the main metric in this paper. S, D and I count substitutions, deletions and insertions needed to turn the speech recogniser's transcript of the Talker audio into the Thinker's text, divided by the number of reference characters. WER is the same on words. Because insertions count, values above one are possible, as in question four of Table 9. You can reuse this metric in your own evaluation.
