§8Putting it into practice

Using MiniMind-O in your own project

  • All three inputs are native. Text (own tokenizer), voice (SenseVoice-Small) and images (SigLIP2, 64 tokens) all enter the same Thinker, and it can answer in text and speech. You do not need an extra speech-to-text model for input; an ASR such as the one the paper uses for evaluation (Qwen3-ASR-Flash) is only needed if you want to score spoken output. No video.
  • Size and Colab. The smallest release is the dense minimind-3o: about 115M trainable parameters plus about 425M frozen (SenseVoice 234M, SigLIP2 94.6M, Mimi 96.2M). That should fit a free T4 (16 GB) even without 4-bit quantization, so plain LoRA or even projector-only training is realistic; QLoRA is optional. Check two things: the T4 has no fast bf16 (the paper trained in bf16 on 24 GB RTX 3090s with batch 32 per GPU, so use fp16 and a smaller batch), and the repo's train_sft_omni.py has no built-in LoRA mode, so adding PEFT adapters is your own step.
  • Where to put LoRA. On the Thinker's attention (GQA q, k, v, o) and FFN layers; train the two small MLP projectors fully (about 1M parameters each, the repo's audio_proj and vision_proj modes); keep SenseVoice, SigLIP2 and Mimi frozen as the paper does. Leave the Talker alone unless you evaluate spoken answers. If you do adapt it, the paper's rank study says the head rank matters more than the embedding rank.
  • Task idea. The training format already has an Audio + Image variant (Fig. 3): a spoken question about a picture gets a text (and speech) answer. The image path is weak (Table 5, animal and vehicle confusions in Fig. 11), so choose a narrow visual task with short answers (e.g. spoken questions about colours, counts or object category in simple photos) and score the text answer with accuracy or F1.
  • Fairness and normalization. The speech-to-speech training data is 70.8% Chinese and only 21.2% English, and longer English answers drift (Table 8, Fig. 10), so compare English against Chinese spoken questions, or seen against unseen voices (Table 7). For normalization, the paper shows numbers written as digits versus words inflate CER (Table 9, q04), so normalize numerals before scoring. Arabic is not tested and the Thinker vocabulary is only 6,400 tokens: check tokenization before using Arabic as a group.
Guide

Use this box as your plan. MiniMind-O already accepts text, voice and images, so you can skip the extra speech model and use its audio plus image format for spoken questions about pictures. The dense model should fit a free T4; add LoRA to the Thinker's attention and feed-forward layers, train the projectors, and keep the encoders frozen. Check fp16 and the missing LoRA mode in the repo first, then compare Chinese and English speakers and normalize numbers before scoring.

Omni: text, image and voice together

Qwen2.5-Omni Technical Report

Jin Xu, Zhifang Guo, Jinzheng He, Hangrui Hu, Ting He, Shuai Bai, Keqin Chen, Jialin Wang, Yang Fan, Kai Dang, Bin Zhang, Xiong Wang, Yunfei Chu, Junyang Lin, et al. · Qwen Team · arXiv 2503.20215v1, March 2025

One 7B model that takes text, images, audio and video (with its sound track) and answers in both text and streaming natural speech. A Thinker (the LLM) reads everything and writes text; a Talker reads the Thinker's hidden states and speaks. A new position scheme, TMRoPE, puts video frames and audio on one shared 40 ms clock.

Size
7B (Thinker from Qwen2.5-7B)
Inputs
text · image · audio · video
Outputs
text + streaming speech
Encoders
ViT ~675M · Whisper-v3 audio
OmniBench avg
56.13% (next best 42.91%)
SEED TTS WER
1.42 / 2.33 / 6.54
Reading guide

Qwen2.5-Omni asks whether one open model can read text, images, audio and video together and answer both in writing and in natural speech, in real time. Its answer is a 7 billion parameter model split into a Thinker, the language model that understands and writes, and a Talker that turns the Thinker's hidden states into streaming speech, with a position scheme called TMRoPE that puts video frames and sound on one clock. The tab starts with the big picture of every input path, then the three problems, the method and training stages, every equation, the four figures redrawn, all ten result tables with three charts, and a box on putting the model into practice. Among the eleven papers it is the second omni model, after MiniMind-O and before Qwen3-Omni, and the one where voice input is fully native.

§0Before you read

This paper assumes you know how pictures and sound are turned into tokens a language model can read, how a model can speak back through "speech tokens", and what a position ID is. With those three ideas, the Thinker, the Talker and TMRoPE all make sense. It is in the atlas because it is the clearest example of a single open model that natively takes text, image and voice, exactly the three inputs a text, image and voice project needs.

Terms used in this paper

Omni model
One model that accepts several kinds of input (here text, image, audio, video) and can answer in more than one form (here text and speech).
Thinker and Talker
The Thinker is the language model that reads everything and writes text. The Talker is a second decoder that reads the Thinker's hidden states and produces speech tokens.
ViT (vision transformer)
A transformer that splits an image into small square patches and turns each patch into a vector, much like words become token vectors.
Log-mel spectrogram
A picture of sound: energy per frequency band over time, on a scale close to human hearing. Here 128 bands, one column every 10 ms.
Whisper-large-v3
OpenAI's open speech-recognition model. Qwen2.5-Omni's audio encoder starts from its weights.
Speech codec tokens
Discrete codes that compress audio so a model can predict speech one token at a time, like text. Qwen's codec is called qwen-tts-tokenizer.
RoPE / TMRoPE
RoPE encodes a token's position by rotating its vector. TMRoPE (time-aligned multimodal RoPE) adds time, height and width IDs so frames and sound share one 40 ms clock.
Flow-matching DiT
A diffusion-style transformer that learns to turn noise into data; here it turns codec tokens into a mel spectrogram.
BigVGAN
A neural vocoder: a network that turns a mel spectrogram into an audio waveform.
Streaming and latency
Streaming means producing output in small chunks as you go; latency is the delay before the first output arrives.
DPO
Direct Preference Optimization: training from pairs of a preferred and a rejected output, without a separate reward model. Used here to make the Talker's speech more stable.
WER
Word error rate: the share of words substituted, deleted or inserted compared with the reference transcript. Lower is better.
OmniBench
A benchmark whose questions need image, audio and text together. Qwen2.5-Omni scores 56.13% on average.
MMMU
A benchmark of college-level exam questions with images across many subjects, used to test image reasoning.
Guide

These fourteen terms are the vocabulary the paper takes for granted. The most important are the Thinker and Talker, the two halves of the model; TMRoPE, its time aligned position scheme; and speech codec tokens, which let a model speak one token at a time. Keep WER in mind too: you will likely report it for voice experiments, and you should normalise transcripts before computing it.

§2Big picture

The Thinker is an ordinary decoder LLM (initialised from Qwen2.5-7B) fed with text tokens, visual tokens and audio tokens. The Talker is a second autoregressive decoder that turns the Thinker's hidden states into speech codec tokens, which a DiT and BigVGAN convert into a waveform chunk by chunk.

§3The problem

  • Sync: video has frames and a sound track on the same clock; the model must know which sound goes with which frame.
  • Interference: training text output and speech output in one stream can make both worse.
  • Streaming: full-attention encoders and a full-sequence vocoder must see the whole input or output before emitting anything, which kills real-time chat.

§4Method

How each input becomes tokens

  1. Text: Qwen's byte-level BPE tokenizer, 151,643 regular tokens.
  2. Audio / voice (also a video's sound track): resample to 16 kHz, 128-channel mel-spectrogram (25 ms window, 10 ms hop), Qwen2-Audio encoder (initialised from Whisper-large-v3); each output frame covers about 40 ms. Attention runs in 2 s blocks so it can stream.
  3. Image: Qwen2.5-VL vision encoder (ViT, about 675M parameters, patch size 14, any resolution); an MLP merges each 2×2 group of patch tokens into one. An image is treated as two identical frames.
  4. Video: frames sampled at a dynamic rate, through the same ViT; its audio goes through the audio encoder.
  5. Positions: TMRoPE gives every token a (temporal, height, width) ID with one temporal ID = 40 ms; video-with-audio is cut into 2 s chunks, vision first, then audio (Fig. 3).
  6. Text out: the Thinker samples text like any LLM (top-p, repetition penalty).
  7. Speech out: the Talker reads Thinker hidden states + sampled text embeddings and emits qwen-tts-tokenizer codes; a sliding-window flow-matching DiT turns codes into mel, BigVGAN turns mel into waveform (Fig. 4).
Guide

This list answers the first practical question: how each modality becomes tokens. Text uses byte-level BPE with about 151 thousand tokens. Audio becomes a 128 channel mel spectrogram and then roughly one token per 40 milliseconds. Images pass through a 675 million parameter vision transformer whose neighbouring patches are merged two by two. Video reuses the same encoder at a dynamic frame rate. TMRoPE then gives everything positions on a shared clock,, and the last two steps produce output.

Post-training data format (paper §4.1 box, transcribed)

<|im_start|>user <|vision_start|>Video.mp4 [Two people are talking in the video]<|vision_end|>What are the people in the video saying?<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant Both pictures are of SpongeBob SquarePants.The person in the red clothes says, "Hello, how's the weather today?" The person in the black clothes responds, "Hello, the weather is quite nice today."<|im_end|> <|im_start|>user <|vision_start|>Video.mp4 [A person in the video is saying, "Please describe the person in front of you."]<|vision_end|><|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant The person in front of you is wearing glasses and a brown jacket over a blue shirt. They appear to be speaking or reacting to something, as their mouth is open and they seem engaged. The background shows a room with a wall-mounted air conditioner, a clothing rack with various garments hanging on it, and a large screen displaying an image of a cityscape at night. The lighting in the room is warm and cozy.<|im_end|>
Guide

This is the paper's example of instruction data in ChatML format, a template you can copy for fine-tuning. Each turn opens with an im start tag and a role, video content sits between vision start and vision end tags, and the assistant's answer ends with im end. Notice that the second user turn has no typed question at all: the question is spoken inside the video, so the model must listen. It is transcribed as printed.

Four latency sources and the fix for each (§2.4)

  1. Input processing: audio encoder attends in 2 s blocks instead of over the whole clip; ViT uses flash attention and 2×2 token merging, so chunked prefill works.
  2. First text to first voice token: the Talker starts from Thinker hidden states while the text is still being written.
  3. First codes to audio: sliding-window block attention in the DiT (lookback 2 blocks, lookahead 1) and chunk-by-chunk BigVGAN.
  4. Architecture cost (model size, FLOPs): listed as a factor; no specific numbers are reported.
Guide

The paper names four delays that add up before a user hears the first sound, and this list pairs each with its fix. Input encoding is made streamable by running audio attention in two second blocks and making the vision encoder efficient. The Talker can start speaking from hidden states while text is still being written. The code-to-wave decoder only looks at a few neighbouring blocks, so audio starts early. The fourth factor, model size, is named but not quantified.

§5Every equation

(1)\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}(\mathcal{P}_\theta;\mathcal{P}_{\text{ref}}) = -\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_w,y_l)\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\log\sigma\left(\beta\log\frac{\mathcal{P}_\theta(y_w\mid x)}{\mathcal{P}_{\text{ref}}(y_w\mid x)} - \beta\log\frac{\mathcal{P}_\theta(y_l\mid x)}{\mathcal{P}_{\text{ref}}(y_l\mid x)}\right)\right] \]

Talker stage 2 (DPO): push the Talker \(\mathcal{P}_\theta\) to prefer the good speech \(y_w\) over the bad \(y_l\) for input text \(x\), relative to the frozen reference \(\mathcal{P}_{\text{ref}}\); \(\beta\) sets strength, \(\sigma\) is the sigmoid. Good/bad are ranked by WER and punctuation-pause error. The only numbered equation in the paper.

Guide

This is the direct preference optimisation loss of the Talker's second stage, the paper's only numbered equation. For input text x, y w is a good speech sample and y l a bad one. The loss rewards the Talker, P theta, for raising the likelihood of the good sample relative to a frozen reference model P ref, more than the bad one; beta sets strength, sigma is the sigmoid. Good and bad are ranked by word error rate and punctuation pause errors.

(text)\[ \text{audio: } (t,h,w) = (k,k,k),\quad k=\left\lfloor \tfrac{\tau}{40\,\text{ms}} \right\rfloor \qquad \text{text: } (t,h,w)=(n,n,n) \]

Not a paper equation: TMRoPE rules from §2.2 written out. Text and audio use identical IDs in all three components (so it reduces to 1D RoPE); for audio the ID is absolute time \(\tau\) in 40 ms steps.

Guide

This is not a paper equation but the TMRoPE rules from section 2.2 written out. Every token gets three position numbers: temporal, height and width. For text and audio all three are equal, which makes it behave like ordinary one dimensional RoPE. For audio the number is absolute time tau divided into 40 millisecond steps, k, so 25 steps make one second. This is what lets sound and video share one clock in figure three.

(text)\[ \text{image / frame } f:\ (t,h,w) = \left(\left\lfloor \tfrac{\tau_f}{40\,\text{ms}}\right\rfloor,\ i,\ j\right),\qquad \text{next modality starts at } \max(\text{previous IDs})+1 \]

Not a paper equation: visual token at row \(i\), column \(j\) of frame \(f\) with timestamp \(\tau_f\). Temporal IDs follow real time even with a variable frame rate (Fig. 3 shows frames 1 s apart getting IDs 0, 25, 50, ...).

Guide

Also written out from the paper's text, not a numbered equation. A visual token in row i and column j of frame f gets height i, width j, and a temporal ID taken from the frame's real timestamp tau f in 40 millisecond steps. Because the ID follows real time, a variable frame rate does not break alignment with audio. When modalities follow each other, the next one starts one past the largest ID used so far.

(text)\[ M_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } i-2 \le j \le i+1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

Not a paper equation: the DiT block attention mask of Fig. 4. Code block \(i\) sees two past blocks, itself and one future block, so the receptive field is 4 blocks.

Guide

This mask, derived from figure four and not printed in the paper, says which code blocks the speech decoder may attend to. M i j is one when block j lies between two blocks before block i and one block after it, and zero otherwise. So each block sees four blocks in total. The small lookahead is why the decoder can start producing audio before the Talker has finished all its codes.

(text)\[ 16\,\text{kHz} \xrightarrow{\text{hop } 10\,\text{ms}} 100 \text{ mel frames/s} \xrightarrow{\text{encoder}} \approx 25 \text{ audio tokens/s} \]

Not a paper equation: token budget implied by §2.2 (10 ms hop, one encoder frame per about 40 ms). A 10 s voice clip costs about 250 tokens.

Guide

A token budget implied by section 2.2, not a paper equation. Audio sampled at 16 kilohertz with a 10 millisecond hop gives 100 mel frames per second, and the encoder outputs about one token per 40 milliseconds, so roughly 25 audio tokens per second. A ten second voice clip therefore costs about 250 tokens. For free Colab experiments this is the number that tells you how much memory voice input will take.

§8Putting it into practice

Using Qwen2.5-Omni in your own fine-tuning project

  • Inputs: text, image, video and voice are all native (voice goes through the Whisper-initialised audio encoder), so you do not need a separate speech-to-text model. You can still add Whisper as an ASR-then-text baseline to compare against native audio input.
  • Size and hardware: the report describes only the 7B model (plus a ~675M ViT, the audio encoder and the Talker). A smaller 3B checkpoint was released after this report: check its model card. Whether 7B QLoRA fits a free T4 (16 GB) is a "check": 4-bit Thinker weights are only a few GB, but visual tokens and about 25 audio tokens per second grow memory fast, so use short clips, small images, and text-only output (skip the Talker). The T4 has no bf16, so run fp16 compute.
  • Where to put LoRA: on the Thinker's attention and MLP projections; keep the ViT, the audio encoder and the Talker frozen. This mirrors the paper's view that the LLM does the reasoning while encoders only perceive.
  • Text + image + voice task: format each sample as a ChatML mixed-modality turn like the §4.1 box (image plus a spoken question, text answer). Table 4 gives you a ready experiment: ask the same question typed and spoken, before and after fine-tuning.
  • Fairness / normalization: ASR quality differs by language (Common Voice WER: zh 5.2, fr 7.5, en 7.6, yue 7.3) and spoken-vs-typed gaps differ by task (CEval much larger than GSM8K). Test accents or languages separately, and normalise transcripts (case, punctuation, numbers) before computing WER; the paper's own DPO reward counts punctuation-pause errors.
Guide

Use this box as a checklist before you start the notebook. Since voice is native, you can skip an extra speech recognizer, but running Whisper as a baseline makes a good comparison. Check memory first: load the smallest checkpoint in four bit, turn off speech output, keep clips short, and put LoRA only on the Thinker's attention and MLP layers. Then build ChatML samples like the paper's example and plan the typed versus spoken and per-language tests.

Omni: text, image and voice together

Qwen3-Omni Technical Report

Qwen Team, Alibaba (core contributors: Jin Xu, Zhifang Guo, Hangrui Hu, Yunfei Chu, Xiong Wang, Jinzheng He, … Junyang Lin) · technical report, arXiv 2509.17765v1 · September 2025 · REFERENCE: larger model

A larger reference model: read it for ideas, not as a model to fine-tune on a small GPU. Qwen3-Omni is a single model that reads text, images, audio and video and answers in text or in streaming speech. A 30B mixture-of-experts "Thinker" (3B active) reads every modality, and a smaller "Talker" turns its hidden states into speech one 80 ms frame at a time. The paper's main claim is that training all modalities together from early pretraining costs nothing on text or vision.

Thinker (LLM)
MoE 30B total · 3B active
Inputs
text · image · audio · video
Outputs
text · streaming speech
First-packet latency
234 ms audio · 547 ms video
Languages
119 text · 19 speech-in · 10 speech-out
Audio benchmarks
open-source SOTA on 32 of 36
Reading guide

Can one model hear, see and read at once without getting worse at any of them? Qwen3-Omni says yes, and it is a larger reference model, read for ideas rather than fine-tuned on a small GPU. A thirty billion parameter mixture-of-experts Thinker, with three billion active per token, reads text, images, audio and video. A smaller Talker turns the Thinker's hidden states into streaming speech. The tab starts with the big picture of every input path. It then covers the problems the paper fixes, the method with its audio encoder, time-aligned positions, streaming speech and training recipe, the relations the paper states in prose, all its figures, all eighteen tables, and a box on putting it into practice. In the atlas it is the ninth of eleven papers: after QLoRA, TinyLLaVA Factory, SmolVLM, Voxtral, Voxtral Realtime, LFM2, MiniMind-O and Qwen2.5-Omni, and before MiniCPM-o 4.5 and Gemma 4.

§0Before you read

This is a larger reference model: read it for ideas, not as a model to train yourself. It shows what a full "omni" model looks like: one model that reads text, images, audio and video and can answer in streaming speech. To follow it you need four ideas: how each input becomes tokens, what a mixture-of-experts model is, how a model can "speak" in codec tokens, and why latency matters. It is useful for understanding how a model handles all three inputs and as a comparison point, even though it is too big to fine-tune on a free T4.

Terms used in this paper

Omni model
A single model that accepts several modalities (here text, image, audio, video) and can reply in more than one (text and speech).
Thinker / Talker
The two halves of the model. The Thinker is the language model that understands the input and writes text; the Talker turns the Thinker's hidden states into speech codes.
Mixture of experts (MoE), 30B-A3B
A layer made of many expert sub-networks with a router that uses only a few per token. 30B-A3B means 30 billion parameters in total, about 3 billion active per token.
Mel spectrogram
A picture of sound: energy in frequency bands spaced like human hearing, computed every few milliseconds (here 128 bands, 10 ms hop).
AuT
Qwen3-Omni's own audio encoder (about 0.6B parameters), trained from scratch on 20 million hours of audio. It outputs one token per 80 ms and replaces Whisper.
RoPE / TM-RoPE
Rotary position embedding tells the model where each token is by rotating its vectors. TM-RoPE gives each token time, height and width positions, with time tied to real timestamps.
Audio codec, codebook
A codec compresses audio into discrete codes. Each frame uses several codebooks: the first captures the coarse sound, the residual ones add detail.
MTP, Code2Wav
MTP (multi-token prediction) is a small module that predicts the residual codebooks for a frame. Code2Wav is the causal decoder that turns those codes into a waveform.
First-packet latency
Time from the end of the user's input to the first piece of audio reply. The paper reports 234 ms for audio input and 547 ms for video on one stream.
Real-time factor (RTF)
Time to generate a stretch of audio divided by its playing time. Below 1 means speech is produced faster than it plays.
WER
Word error rate: the share of words a transcript gets wrong (substituted, deleted or inserted). Lower is better; it depends on how text is normalized before scoring.
MMMU, MMAU, VoiceBench
Benchmarks: MMMU tests college-level questions about images, MMAU tests audio understanding and reasoning, VoiceBench tests answering spoken instructions.
FLEURS
A multilingual read-speech dataset used here for speech recognition (WER) and speech translation (BLEU) across many languages.
vLLM
An open-source serving engine for fast language-model inference; the paper measures latency with it.
Guide

Keep this glossary open while you read the tab. The terms you will meet most often are Thinker and Talker, mixture of experts, AuT, TM-RoPE and codebook. For your experiments, word error rate matters most: it counts wrong words in a transcript, and its value changes with how you normalize text, which is the point of a with and without normalization experiment. The benchmark names tell you which modality each table tests.

§2Big picture

All three common inputs (text, image, voice) are native, so no speech-to-text step is needed. The part that is new here is on the output side (the streaming Talker) and in the time alignment (TM-RoPE).

§3The problem

  • Modality trade-off: LLM-centric multimodal models often get better at one modality and worse at another.
  • Audio encoder: Qwen2.5-Omni used Whisper. Qwen3-Omni replaces it with AuT, trained from scratch on 20 million hours of audio, and handles inputs longer than 40 minutes.
  • Positions: M-RoPE put time on the first 16 (high-frequency) rotary angles, which hurts extrapolation to long sequences. Qwen2.5-Omni also cut audio-video into fixed 2-second chunks.
  • Latency under load: dense models and block-wise synthesis get slow when many users stream at once.

§4Method

How each input becomes tokens

  1. Text: Qwen's byte-level BPE tokenizer (151,643 regular tokens) turns text into ids, and the Thinker's embedding table turns ids into vectors.
  2. Image: the Qwen3-VL vision encoder (initialized from SigLIP2-So400m, about 543M parameters) turns the image into visual tokens. An adapter maps them to the Thinker's width.
  3. Video: frames are sampled at a dynamic frame rate and go through the same vision encoder. Each frame's time id follows its real timestamp (80 ms per id). The soundtrack is taken out and sent to the audio path.
  4. Voice / audio: 16 kHz audio becomes a 128-bin mel spectrogram, then AuT encoder tokens at 12.5 Hz, then an adapter.
  5. Fuse: TM-RoPE positions all tokens on a shared time axis, and the MoE Thinker reads them as one sequence and writes text.
  6. Speak (optional): the Talker reads the Thinker's multimodal hidden states and the streamed text, predicts codebook 0 per frame, the MTP module adds the residual codebooks, and Code2Wav renders 80 ms of waveform.
Guide

These six steps follow one request from raw input to answer. Text is tokenized, images and video pass through the shared vision encoder, and voice passes through the mel front end and AuT. TM-RoPE then puts everything on one time axis so the Thinker can read a single sequence. Speaking is an optional last step for the Talker. This list is also the skeleton of a one-page explanation of the inputs.

Streaming speech: Talker, MTP, Code2Wav

Streaming speech loop (our sketch of Sec. 2.4–2.5; not an algorithm box in the paper) context ← Thinker multimodal hidden states + streamed text for frame k = 1, 2, … : h_k ← Talker(context, e_1 … e_{k-1}) # MoE, 12.5 frames/s c_k,0 ← sample(LinearHead(h_k)) # zeroth codebook c_k,1..J ← MTP(h_k, c_k,0) # fixed-step, dense 80M e_k ← Σ_j Embed_j(c_k,j) # aggregated codec feature audio_k ← Code2Wav(e_1 … e_k) # causal ConvNet, left context emit audio_k (80 ms) # first packet after k = 1
Guide

This loop is our sketch of sections two point four and two point five, not an algorithm box from the paper. The Talker is conditioned once on the Thinker's context, then loops over frames. In each pass it samples codebook zero, lets the small MTP module add the residual codes, sums their embeddings, and hands them to Code2Wav, which emits eighty milliseconds of audio right away. The same logic appears as equation five and in the streaming Talker diagram.

Training recipe

  1. S1 Encoder alignment: LLM frozen (from Qwen3), vision encoder from Qwen3-VL, audio encoder from AuT. Train adapters first, then encoders.
  2. S2 General: all parameters trained on about 2 trillion tokens (text 0.57T, audio 0.77T, image 0.82T, video 0.05T, video-audio 0.05T), with unimodal and cross-modal data mixed from the start.
  3. S3 Long context: maximum length raised from 8,192 to 32,768 tokens, with more long audio and video.
  4. Thinker post-training: light SFT in ChatML format, then strong-to-weak distillation (off-policy from teacher outputs, then on-policy matching the logits of Qwen3-32B or Qwen3-235B-A22B via KL), then GSPO with rule-based rewards and LLM-as-judge rewards (Qwen3; Qwen2.5-VL for visual tasks).
  5. Talker training: (1) map multimodal representations to speech on hundreds of millions of clips, (2) continual pretraining on high-quality data plus long-context training, (3) DPO on multilingual preference pairs, (4) speaker fine-tuning for specific voices.
  6. Captioner: Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B fine-tuned on detailed audio descriptions (qualitative results in Appendix 9.2).
Guide

The training recipe runs in three phases. Pre-training aligns the encoders to a frozen language model, then trains everything on mixed data, then stretches the context. The Thinker is post-trained with supervised fine-tuning, distillation from larger Qwen3 teachers and reinforcement learning with rule-based and judge-based rewards. The Talker gets its own four stages ending in speaker fine-tuning. The Captioner shows that the released model can be fine-tuned further for a new task.

§5Every equation

The report has no numbered equations. Below are the quantitative relations it states in prose, written as display math (labels i–vii are ours). Where the notation is ours, the note says so.

(i)\[ f_{\text{tok}} = \frac{1}{8 \times 10\ \text{ms}} = 12.5\ \text{Hz}, \qquad 40\ \text{min} \times 60 \times 12.5 \approx 30{,}000\ \text{audio tokens} \]

Audio token rate: a 10 ms mel hop, downsampled 8 times by AuT's Conv2d blocks, gives one token per 80 ms. The 40-minute token count is our arithmetic.

Guide

Relation one computes the audio token rate. One divided by eight times ten milliseconds gives twelve and a half tokens per second, so each token covers eighty milliseconds. Multiply forty minutes by sixty seconds by twelve and a half and you get about thirty thousand tokens, our own arithmetic. Use the same calculation to estimate sequence lengths for your voice clips before you fine-tune.

(ii)\[ \underbrace{64}_{\text{rotary angles}} = \underbrace{24}_{t} + \underbrace{20}_{h} + \underbrace{20}_{w} \quad \text{(interleaved)} \qquad \text{vs. M-RoPE: } t \leftarrow \text{angles } 1\ldots16 \]

TM-RoPE angle allocation: time, height and width share the rotary frequencies in an interleaved pattern, so time is no longer only on the highest frequencies.

Guide

Relation two is the TM-RoPE budget. Sixty-four rotary angles are shared as twenty-four for time t, twenty for height h and twenty for width w, and they are interleaved rather than stacked in blocks. Under M-RoPE, time used only angles one to sixteen. Spreading time across fast and slow frequencies is what the paper credits for better handling of long audio and video.

(iii)\[ \text{text: } (t,h,w) = (n,n,n) \quad \text{image: } (s,\ s+r,\ s+c) \quad \text{audio/video: } t = s + \left\lfloor \tfrac{\tau}{80\ \text{ms}} \right\rfloor \]

Position ids per modality: n is the token index, r and c are the patch row and column, τ is the real timestamp, and s is the modality's start offset. The exact offset form for h and w is our reading of the M-RoPE convention.

Guide

Relation three gives the position ids for each modality. For text, t, h and w all equal the token index n, which reduces to ordinary one-dimensional RoPE. For an image, time is a fixed start value s, and height and width add the patch row r and column c. For audio and video, time is s plus the real timestamp tau divided by eighty milliseconds. The image offset is our reading of M-RoPE, so treat it as approximate.

(iv)\[ s_{m+1} = 1 + \max \operatorname{pos}(m) \]

Contiguous numbering: each new modality starts one past the largest position id of the one before, so ids never collide.

Guide

Relation four keeps positions from colliding. The start offset of the next modality, s sub m plus one, is one more than the largest position id used by the previous modality m. This is the dashed arrow in the TM-RoPE diagram.

(v)\[ e_k = \sum_{j=0}^{J} E_j\!\left[c_{k,j}\right], \qquad c_{k,0} \sim \operatorname{softmax}(W_0 h_k), \qquad c_{k,1:J} = \operatorname{MTP}(h_k, c_{k,0}) \]

Multi-codebook frame (our notation): the Talker's linear head gives codebook 0, the MTP module gives the J residual codebooks (J = 15 in Fig. 2), and the summed embedding ek goes to Code2Wav and back into the Talker.

Guide

Relation five, in our notation, describes one speech frame. The frame embedding e sub k is the sum over codebooks j from zero to J of each codebook's embedding table E sub j applied to its chosen code c. The zeroth code is sampled from a softmax over a linear head on the Talker state h sub k. The MTP module predicts the remaining J codes, fifteen in Figure two, and the sum feeds Code2Wav and the next Talker step.

(vi)\[ L_{\text{first}} = L_{\text{pre}} + \text{TTFT}_{\text{Thinker}} + \text{TTFT}_{\text{Talker}} + t_{\text{MTP}} + t_{\text{codec}} = 72 + 88 + 57 + 14 + 3 = 234\ \text{ms} \]

First-packet latency is the sum of sequential stages (Table 2, audio, one stream). For video: 160 + 160 + 210 + 14 + 3 = 547 ms.

Guide

Relation six says first-packet latency is simply a sum, because the stages run one after another: pre-processing, the Thinker's time to first token, the Talker's time to first token, one MTP step and one codec step. With one audio stream that is seventy-two plus eighty-eight plus fifty-seven plus fourteen plus three, which equals two hundred thirty-four milliseconds. The same check for video gives five hundred forty-seven.

(vii)\[ \text{RTF} = \frac{t_{\text{Thinker}} + t_{\text{Talker}} + t_{\text{MTP}} + t_{\text{codec}}}{80\ \text{ms}} \lt 1, \qquad \tfrac{1000}{75} + \tfrac{1000}{140} + 14 + 3 \approx 37.5\ \text{ms} \Rightarrow 0.47 \]

Real-time factor: the time to produce one 80 ms frame divided by 80 ms. Below 1 means speech is produced faster than it plays. The check with Table 2's single-stream rates is ours.

Guide

Relation seven is the real-time factor: the time to produce one frame, Thinker token plus Talker token plus MTP plus codec, divided by the eighty milliseconds that frame lasts. Below one means speech is generated faster than it plays. With Table two's single-stream rates, about thirteen plus seven plus fourteen plus three milliseconds gives about thirty-seven and a half, a factor of about zero point four seven, matching the paper. The check is ours.

(viii)\[ \min_{\theta}\ \sum_t D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(p_{\text{teacher}}(\cdot \mid x, y_{\lt t}) \,\Vert\, p_{\theta}(\cdot \mid x, y_{\lt t})\right), \quad y \sim p_{\theta} \]

On-policy distillation: the student samples y, and its logits are pulled toward the teacher's (Qwen3-32B or 235B-A22B). The paper only says "minimizing the KL divergence", so the KL direction shown is an assumption.

Guide

Relation eight is on-policy distillation. The student samples its own answer y, and at each step t its next-token distribution p theta is pulled toward the teacher's by minimising the KL divergence. The teacher is Qwen3 thirty-two B or the two hundred thirty-five billion parameter model. The paper does not state the direction of the KL, so the order shown is an assumption. This is the second stage of Thinker post-training.

§8Putting it into practice

Qwen3-Omni in a fine-tuning project (REFERENCE: a larger model)

  • This is a larger reference model, not a small model to fine-tune. Read it to understand what a full "omni" model looks like. It accepts text, image and voice natively (text, image, voice, plus video), so you would not need a speech-to-text pipeline. It also produces speech.
  • Too big for a free T4. Every released variant (Instruct, Thinking, Captioner) is 30B-A3B. Although only 3B parameters are active per token, all 30B Thinker weights must be in memory. At 4 bits that is already about 15 GB before the encoders (about 1.2B), the Talker stack, activations and LoRA states. QLoRA on a 16 GB Colab T4 is therefore not realistic. Check the model card if you want to try, and plan to use a smaller omni model instead (for example the Qwen2.5-Omni 3B/7B in the next tab) or rent a larger cloud GPU. The "Flash" models in the tables are in-house and not released.
  • Where LoRA would go: on the Thinker's attention projections (q, k, v, o). Keep AuT and the vision encoder frozen. The paper's own S1 trains adapters before encoders and warns that encoders compensate badly for a frozen LLM. Leave the Talker off or frozen if your task only needs text answers. Adapters on every MoE expert multiply the parameter count, so check which modules your library targets.
  • Task idea from the paper: spoken questions about an image or video (VoiceBench-style spoken instructions plus vision). The paper argues end-to-end models beat cascaded pipelines on latency and cross-modal reasoning. If your own model needs a cascade (ASR, then a VLM), that claim is a good comparison point in your report.
  • Fairness and normalization angles: speech input covers 19 languages including Arabic and Urdu, but speech output does not include Arabic, and the paper only reports a 19-language Fleurs average (5.33 WER), not per-language numbers. An Arabic vs English gap therefore has to be measured yourself. On normalization, the paper converts lyric transcripts to Simplified Chinese before scoring and highlights Japanese scored "without text normalization" (Table 15). WER depends on how you normalize, so a with and without normalization experiment is well worth running.
Guide

Use this paper as a map, not as your model. It handles text, image and voice inputs natively, but every released variant is thirty billion parameters, too large for QLoRA on a free sixteen gigabyte T four, so pick a smaller model such as Qwen two point five Omni. Borrow the ideas instead: LoRA on attention with frozen encoders, a spoken-question-about-an-image task, and a fairness test on Arabic versus English, where this paper reports no per-language numbers.

Omni: text, image and voice together

MiniCPM-o 4.5: Towards Real-Time Full-Duplex Omni-Modal Interaction

Junbo Cui, Bokai Xu, Chongyi Wang, Tianyu Yu, … Maosong Sun, Zhiyuan Liu, Yuan Yao · MiniCPM-o Team, OpenBMB · arXiv 2604.27393, April 2026

A 9B open model that sees (images, video), hears (speech, sounds) and speaks back at the same time. A SigLIP vision encoder and a Whisper audio encoder feed a Qwen3-8B language model; a small speech decoder turns the LLM's hidden states into voice. The key idea, Omni-Flow, cuts the conversation into 1-second chunks so the model keeps listening and watching while it talks, and can decide on its own when to speak.

Parameters
9.34B (LLM: Qwen3-8B)
Inputs
text · image · video · audio
Outputs
text + streaming speech
Visual tokens
64 per slice (16× compression)
Audio tokens
10 per second
Memory (INT4 inference)
11 GB
Reading guide

MiniCPM-o 4.5 asks how a small open model can see, listen and speak at the same time, instead of taking turns like a walkie-talkie. Its answer is a nine billion parameter model that turns images, video and audio into tokens for a Qwen3 eight B language model, and a framework called Omni-Flow that cuts the live stream into one-second chunks so the model reads new input and writes its reply in every chunk. The tab moves from the big picture of every input path, through the problem, the method, every equation and figure, to the result tables and a box on putting it into practice. In the atlas it is the tenth of eleven papers, in the omni group after MiniMind-O, Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni, and just before Gemma 4. For a text, image and voice project, it is a clean example where all three inputs are native.

§0Before you read

To follow this paper you need three ideas: how pictures and sound are turned into tokens a language model can read, what "full-duplex" streaming means (listening and talking at the same time), and how a model produces speech from text. MiniCPM-o 4.5 takes all three common inputs (text, image and voice) natively in one 9B model, so it is a clean example of every input path, and for fine-tuning its document and spoken-question skills suggest a good task.

Terms used in this paper

Omni-modal
A model that takes several kinds of input (text, images, video, audio) in one network, and here can also answer in speech.
Full-duplex vs simplex
Full-duplex means the model keeps perceiving while it talks, like a phone call. Simplex (turn-based) means it listens, then answers, then listens again.
Omni-Flow and [listen]
The paper's framework that splits a live stream into 1-second chunks of visual, audio and output tokens. Outputting [listen] means "stay silent this second".
Qwen3-8B (backbone)
The 8-billion-parameter open language model at the centre. It reads every token and writes the text answer; this is where you would put LoRA adapters.
SigLIP ViT and resampler
SigLIP is a vision transformer trained on image–text pairs; it turns 14×14-pixel patches into vectors. The resampler uses 64 learned queries to compress 1024 vectors per slice to 64 tokens.
Whisper encoder, log-mel spectrogram
Whisper is OpenAI's speech-recognition model; only its encoder is reused here. Its input is a log-mel spectrogram: loudness in 80 frequency bands over time, on a scale close to human hearing.
S3 speech tokens
Discrete speech codes from the CosyVoice speech tokenizer: 25 per second, each one of 6,562 codebook entries. The small speech decoder predicts them.
Flow-matching decoder
A generative model that turns speech tokens into an audio waveform, in streaming fashion, copying the voice of a short reference recording.
TAIL
The paper's rule for training data: each text token is placed in the 1-second chunk in which it starts being spoken, so the speech stays in step with real time.
WER / CER
Word error rate and character error rate: the share of words (or characters, used for Chinese) that are wrong in a transcript. Lower is better.
SIM-o
Speaker similarity between the generated speech and the reference voice, measured with a speaker-verification model. Higher is better.
Benchmarks: MMMU, OCRBench, OmniDocBench, LibriSpeech
Standard tests: MMMU is college-level image questions, OCRBench and OmniDocBench test reading text and documents in images (OmniDocBench is an edit distance, lower is better), LibriSpeech is English audiobook speech for WER.
INT4, BF16, RTX 4090
BF16 stores each weight in 16 bits, INT4 in 4 bits. The paper measures speed on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 (24 GB): 19 GB in BF16, 11 GB in INT4, versus 16 GB on a free Colab T4.
RTF (real-time factor)
Processing time divided by the length of the audio. Below 1 means the model runs faster than real time, which live conversation needs.
Guide

Keep this list open while you read. The most important terms are full-duplex, meaning the model listens while it talks, Omni-Flow with its listen token, and the chain from Whisper and SigLIP into the Qwen3 eight B backbone. For your experiments, note word error rate, which you may use as a metric, and the memory figures: for inference, sixteen bit weights need nineteen gigabytes, while four bit weights fit in eleven.

§2Big picture

Everything from the encoders to the speech token decoder (about 9B parameters) is connected by hidden states, so gradients flow end to end. Omni-Flow interleaves the streams in 1-second chunks so the model can listen, watch and talk at once. It also runs in ordinary turn-based mode.

§3The problem

  • Blocked I/O: perception and response alternate, so new input cannot change an answer mid-sentence.
  • Passive: the model only answers explicit requests; it never speaks up on its own (e.g. a reminder).
  • Cost of speech: letting the LLM produce 25 speech tokens per second slows it and degrades language ability [13, 14].
  • Lag: how long a text token takes to say varies, so a fixed text-to-speech ratio drifts from real time.

§4Method

How each input is processed

  1. Image: LLaVA-UHD splits the image into slices (max 2240×2240, or 448×448 in full-duplex mode); SigLIP ViT (27 layers, patch 14) turns each slice into 1024 tokens; a 64-query resampler compresses them to 64 tokens (16×, vs the usual 4×).
  2. Video: frames are sampled (SFT uses 1–5 fps, 0.2–0.4 megapixel) and each frame follows the image path; in streaming, frames of each 1 s chunk become the visual tokens v.
  3. Audio: a Whisper-medium encoder (80 mel bins, 24 layers) encodes audio chunk by chunk at 50 tokens/s; a two-layer MLP (1024→4096→4096) merges every 5 into one, giving 10 tokens/s.
  4. Text: the Qwen3-8B backbone reads the interleaved sequence and writes text tokens (3–4 per second in real time).
  5. Speech out: for each text token, its LLM hidden state (via an MLP, 4096→768) is added to its embedding in a 0.3B Llama-style speech token decoder, which emits S3 speech tokens (25/s, codebook 6,562); a streaming flow-matching decoder turns them into a waveform in the voice of the reference audio.
Guide

These five steps are the whole input story in compact form: how text, image, video and voice each enter the model and how speech comes out. The logic is the same for every modality. A pretrained encoder turns raw signal into features, a small projector compresses them into a few tokens the language model can read, and the language model does the reasoning. Speech output reverses the idea, with the model's hidden states steering a small speech decoder.

TAIL supervision and look-ahead (§3.4), as a procedure

Procedure (described in text; the paper has no Algorithm box) Input: full-duplex sample with start/end time of every text token, chunk size t for k = 1, 2, ... : text_k ← text tokens whose start time ∈ [(k−1)t, kt) speech_k ← speech tokens of text_k defer speech of the last few tokens of text_k to chunk k+1 # look-ahead ("the apple") o_k ← interleave(text_k, speech_k) # number of text tokens varies per chunk g_k ← [v_k ; a_k ; o_k] # [listen] if nothing to say train with next-token prediction on g_1 g_2 ... g_K → model learns to write fewer text tokens when playback is behind kt
Guide

This procedure shows how the training data for time-aligned speech is built. For each one-second chunk, collect the text tokens that start being spoken in that second, attach their speech tokens, and push the speech of the last few tokens into the next chunk so pronunciation can see the next word. Because the amount of text per chunk varies, the model learns to write less when its voice is running behind.

§5Every equation

—\[ \mathbf{g}_k = [\mathbf{v}^k;\ \mathbf{a}^k;\ \mathbf{o}^k], \qquad \text{sequence} = \mathbf{g}_1\,\mathbf{g}_2\,\mathbf{g}_3\cdots \]

§3.2 Unified serialization: chunk k holds visual tokens v, audio tokens a and output tokens o (only [listen] if silent); groups are concatenated for a causal LM.

Guide

g k equals the list of v k, a k and o k: the visual tokens, audio tokens and output tokens of chunk k. The full sequence is simply g one, g two, g three and so on, one after the other. This single line is how the paper turns a continuous live conversation into something a normal causal language model can read and train on, as drawn in the Omni-Flow diagram.

—\[ \text{text token } j \in \text{chunk } k \iff t^{\text{start}}_j \in [(k-1)t,\ kt) \]

§3.4 TAIL: text tokens (with their speech tokens) are assigned to the chunk in which they start being spoken; t is the chunk duration (1 s).

Guide

A text token j belongs to chunk k exactly when its start time falls between k minus one times t and k times t, where t is the chunk length of one second. This is the rule behind TAIL. It ties each word to the second in which it is actually spoken, so the model's text and its voice stay on the same clock.

—\[ 50\ \tfrac{\text{tokens}}{\text{s}} \xrightarrow{\ \text{MLP},\ 5\times\ } 10\ \tfrac{\text{tokens}}{\text{s}}, \qquad 1024 \xrightarrow{\ \text{resampler},\ 16\times\ } 64\ \text{tokens/slice} \]

§2 Token budgets for audio and images (numbers from the text, written as display math here).

Guide

These two token budgets explain why the model is cheap enough for streaming. Audio goes from 50 Whisper tokens per second to 10 after a five times merge by the MLP. Each image slice goes from 1024 SigLIP tokens to 64 after the resampler, a sixteen times compression where many models use four. Fewer tokens also means shorter sequences and less memory when you fine-tune.

(1)\[ r_{\text{len}}(i)=\begin{cases} s_i, & r_i=1,\\ \min(0,s_i), & r_i=0,\end{cases}\qquad s_i=\left(0.5-\frac{\ell_i-\ell_{\min}}{\ell_{\max}-\ell_{\min}}\right)\times\min\!\left(1,\frac{\ell_{\max}-\ell_{\min}}{\tau}\right) \]

Smooth length reward for RL (adapted from Kimi-K1.5): ri = correct or not; ℓi, ℓmin, ℓmax = lengths of responses to the same prompt; short correct answers get up to +0.5; wrong answers are never rewarded for being short; τ shrinks the reward when lengths barely differ. Not used for the first 480 steps.

Guide

Equation one is the length reward used in reinforcement learning. For each prompt, s i is 0.5 minus the response length rescaled between the shortest and longest answer, times a factor that shrinks when lengths barely differ, controlled by tau. Correct answers get s i, so short correct answers earn up to half a point. Wrong answers get the minimum of zero and s i, so being short never rescues a wrong answer.

MiniCPM-o is close to the best at recognition and wins GigaSpeech and VoxPopuli, and it leads clearly on Speech TriviaQA with 75.5. It trails on Speech Web Questions and Chinese knowledge questions. For your own project, this means spoken questions are understood well without a separate speech-to-text model.

This ablation compares three length rewards in reinforcement learning, showing benchmark average and how much shorter the answers became. §8Putting it into practice

  • Inputs: text, images (and video frames) and audio/voice are all native, so no extra speech-to-text model is needed. It can also answer in speech, but for fine-tuning a text answer is easier to score.
  • Size and GPU: the paper describes only the 9B model (9.34B parameters), with no smaller variant. BF16 inference already needs 19 GB (Table 11), so it will not fit a 16 GB T4. With 4-bit loading, inference used 11–14 GB; QLoRA on a free T4 or Kaggle's 2×T4 is plausible but not shown in the paper, so check. Use short audio clips and one image slice (448×448) to keep sequences short.
  • Where to put LoRA: on the Qwen3-8B attention and MLP projections (q, k, v, o, gate, up, down). Keep SigLIP, Whisper and the speech decoders frozen, and skip loading the speech-output modules if you only need text. The small audio projector (21M) and resampler (89M) are the modules the paper trains first when a new modality is added (stage 1 trains the new projectors); unfreeze them only if your audio or images are very different from normal.
  • Task idea: the model is strongest on documents and OCR (best OmniDocBench) and on spoken QA (Speech TriviaQA 75.5), so "spoken question about a photo of a document or chart" fits well. Score with exact match or F1 on the text answer.
  • Fairness and normalization: ASR is reported mostly for Chinese and English, and the authors admit English–Chinese mixing in speech. Compare two speaker groups or two languages (e.g. English vs Arabic questions; the paper gives no Arabic results). For normalization, lowercase, strip punctuation and write numbers one way before computing WER or exact match, as the reference answers and the model's text may differ only in form.
Guide

Use this box to plan your fine-tuning and experiments. All three inputs are native, so you can skip a speech-to-text pipeline. The main risk is memory: load the model in four bits, freeze the encoders, put LoRA on the backbone's attention and MLP layers, and test on a T4 early. A spoken question about a document photo plays to its strengths, and an English versus Arabic comparison gives a clear fairness experiment.

Omni: text, image and voice together

Gemma 4 Technical Report

Gemma Team, Google DeepMind · arXiv 2607.02770 (v2, 24 Jul 2026) · 2026 · Apache 2.0 weights

Gemma 4 is a family of open decoder-only models (2.3B effective up to 31B, plus a 26B Mixture-of-Experts) that read text, images and audio and answer in text. The small E2B and E4B models attach a frozen ViT image encoder and a frozen USM-style audio encoder to the language model. The 12B model drops both encoders and projects raw image patches and raw 40 ms audio chunks straight into the LLM with small linear layers.

Sizes
E2B · E4B · 12B · 26B-A4B · 31B
Inputs
text + image (all) · audio (E2B, E4B, 12B)
Output
text only (optional thinking trace)
Image encoder
ViT 150M / 550M, patch 16
Audio encoder
305M Conformer, 40 ms chunks
Smallest model
E2B: 4.6 GB bf16 (text weights)
Reading guide

Gemma 4 asks how far a family of open models can go in reading text, images and audio while staying small enough for phones and free GPUs. The answer is a set of decoder-only models, from E2B with 2.3 billion effective parameters up to a 31 billion dense model and a 26 billion Mixture-of-Experts, that take all three inputs and reply in text. The small models attach frozen image and audio encoders, and the 12B model drops the encoders entirely. The tab opens with the input paths, then the problems, the method with Algorithm 1, the display math, the two figures, all twelve tables, and a box on putting it into practice. Gemma 4 is the last of the eleven papers, after MiniCPM-o 4.5, and closes the omni group that started with MiniMind-O.

§0Before you read

Gemma 4 closes the atlas and is probably the most practical base model for a hands-on fine-tuning project: its small E2B and E4B models take text, images and speech natively and fit a free 16 GB T4. To follow the paper you need three ideas: how a picture and a sound become tokens for a language model, what "effective" and "active" parameter counts mean, and how much GPU memory each size needs. The paper's headline, the encoder-free 12B model, is a shortcut through the first idea.

Terms used in this paper

E2B, E4B (effective parameters)
Names of the two smallest models. "Effective" counts the parameters doing the heavy compute; per-layer embedding tables are stored on top, so E2B holds about 5 billion parameters but behaves like a 2.3 billion model.
Mixture-of-Experts (26B-A4B)
A model whose feed-forward layers are split into many "experts"; a router sends each token to only a few. 26B-A4B stores 26 billion parameters but uses about 4 billion per token.
ViT and soft tokens
A Vision Transformer cuts an image into 16-pixel patches and encodes each one. After pooling, the resulting vectors, called soft tokens, are placed in the prompt like words. Gemma 4 lets you pick 70 to 1120 of them per image.
Mel filterbank
A standard audio feature: short slices of sound turned into energy per frequency band, with bands spaced the way human hearing works. It is the input of the audio encoder in E2B and E4B.
Conformer (USM)
A Transformer with added convolution layers, good at speech. Gemma 4's 305M audio encoder uses twelve Conformer layers in the style of Google's Universal Speech Model.
Encoder-free
The 12B design: no separate image or audio network, only a small linear projection from raw pixels or raw audio samples into the language model.
KV cache, local and global attention
The KV cache stores keys and values of past tokens so they are not recomputed. Local layers look only at a recent window; one global layer in every five or six sees everything, which keeps the cache small.
Thinking mode
An option in which the model first writes a reasoning trace, then its answer. It is switched on with a control token in the chat template.
MTP drafter (speculative decoding)
A small extra network that guesses the next few tokens; the main model checks them all in one pass and keeps the correct ones. It speeds up generation without changing the answers.
QAT, bf16, Q4_0
bf16 stores each weight in two bytes. Quantization-aware training teaches the model to cope with low-bit weights, so the released four-bit files, such as the Q4_0 format used by llama.cpp, lose little quality.
WER and CER
Word and character error rate: the share of words or characters a transcript gets wrong, lower is better. CER is used for Chinese, Japanese and Korean.
FLEURS and CoVoST
Speech benchmarks. FLEURS measures transcription in many languages, scored with WER; CoVoST measures speech translation into English, scored with BLEU, where higher is better.
InfographicVQA, MMMU Pro
Image benchmarks. InfographicVQA asks questions about charts and posters full of text; MMMU Pro asks university-level multiple-choice questions that need an image.
TPU
Google's own AI accelerator chip, used here for pre-training on thousands of chips. You will fine-tune on an NVIDIA T4 instead.
Guide

These fourteen terms are the vocabulary the paper assumes. Model names carry meaning: E2B means about two billion effective parameters, and A4B means about four billion active parameters in a Mixture-of-Experts. Soft tokens, Mel filterbanks and Conformers describe how images and sound get in. WER, CER, BLEU, FLEURS and CoVoST are how the paper scores speech, and you will reuse WER in your own evaluation. Come back here whenever a table uses a name you do not know.

§2Big picture

All modalities become vectors in the same embedding space and are read by one decoder. Encoders are frozen; the decoder is what gets trained. Which inputs you get depends on the size you pick.

§3The problem

  • Separate encoders are heavy. In Gemma 3n the audio encoder was 680M parameters (390 MB on disk); it has to run before the LLM even sees the audio.
  • Long context explodes the KV cache. Every global-attention layer stores keys and values for every past token.
  • Images come in every shape. A fixed square resize distorts documents and wastes tokens; the budget must be set per image.
  • Decoding is slow token by token. This motivates the speculative MTP drafter.

§4Method

How one multimodal prompt flows through Gemma 4

  1. Format the turn. Wrap the conversation in control tokens (<|turn>user … <turn|>); add <|think|> in the system turn to switch on thinking (Table 11).
  2. Text is split by the SentencePiece tokenizer (262k entries, split digits, preserved whitespace, byte fallback) and embedded; E2B/E4B also add per-layer embeddings.
  3. Images are resized with Algorithm 1 so the number of soft tokens stays under \(N_{\max}\in\{70,140,280,560,1120\}\), cut into 16×16 patches, encoded by the frozen ViT, and pooled 3×3 into soft tokens.
  4. Audio (E2B/E4B) becomes Mel filterbank features in 40 ms chunks, passes 2 downsampling convolutions and 12 Conformer layers, and enters the LLM as continuous vectors. In 12B, raw 640-sample chunks are projected linearly.
  5. The decoder runs 5 sliding-window local layers per global layer (4:1 in E2B), with RoPE (base 10k) on local and p-RoPE (p = 0.25, base 1M) on global layers.
  6. Generation: optional thought trace in <|channel>thought … <channel|>, then the answer; the MTP drafter proposes several tokens that the main model verifies.
Guide

These six steps follow one prompt through the model. First the conversation is wrapped in turn tokens. Then text is tokenized, images are resized and pooled into soft tokens, and audio is encoded in 40 millisecond chunks. All of these vectors enter the same decoder, which mixes local and global attention. Finally the model may write a thinking trace before its answer, while the drafter speeds up decoding. It is the skeleton of a one-page explanation of the inputs.

Algorithm 1 Aspect-Ratio Preserving Image Resizing (see also Figure 2) Require: image I ∈ R^(H×W×C), patch size p, max tokens N_max, pooling kernel size k 1: m ← k · p ▷ pooled patch size 2: T ← N_max · m² 3: f ← sqrt( T / (H · W) ) ▷ ideal scaling factor 4: H_ideal ← f · H 5: W_ideal ← f · W 6: H_target ← ⌊H_ideal / m⌋ · m ▷ round down 7: W_target ← ⌊W_ideal / m⌋ · m 8: I_resized ← BicubicResize(I, H_target, W_target) 9: return I_resized
Guide

Algorithm 1 picks an image size that respects the token budget while keeping the shape. It computes the side of one pooled patch, the pixel area the budget allows, and a single scale factor for both sides. Then it rounds each side down to whole pooled patches, so the budget is never exceeded, and resizes bicubically. Figure 2 runs this procedure on a real example.

§5Every equation

The report has no numbered equations. Below is its display math: the lines of Algorithm 1, a worked example with the Figure 2 numbers, and the few quantities stated in the text.

Alg. 1\[ m = k\cdot p, \qquad T = N_{\max}\, m^{2}, \qquad f=\sqrt{\frac{T}{H\,W}} \]

m is the side of one pooled patch (k×k ViT patches of p pixels); T is the pixel area allowed by the token budget; f scales the image so H·W ≈ T.

Guide

The first three lines of Algorithm 1. m equals k times p: the side of a pooled patch, k by k patches of p pixels each. T equals N max times m squared: the pixel area the token budget allows. f is the square root of T over H times W: one scale factor applied to both height and width so the area lands near T.

Alg. 1\[ H_{\text{target}}=\left\lfloor \frac{f H}{m}\right\rfloor m,\qquad W_{\text{target}}=\left\lfloor \frac{f W}{m}\right\rfloor m \]

Round each side down to a whole number of pooled patches, so the soft-token count never exceeds Nmax; then resize bicubically.

Guide

Rounding down is what keeps the image within budget. H target is f times H divided by m, rounded down to a whole number, times m, and the same for the width. Because both sides shrink to whole pooled patches, the number of soft tokens can only be at or below N max. The aspect ratio is kept mostly, not exactly.

—\[ N_{\text{soft}}=\frac{H_{\text{target}}}{m}\cdot\frac{W_{\text{target}}}{m}\le N_{\max},\qquad N_{\text{patch}} = k^{2} N_{\text{soft}} \]

Soft tokens the LLM sees, and ViT patches the encoder processes (implied by the pooling described in Fig. 2).

Guide

The soft-token count is the number of pooled patches along the height times the number along the width, and it never exceeds N max. The ViT itself sees k squared times as many patches, nine times more with a three by three pool. This line is implied by Figure 2 rather than printed in the paper.

Fig. 2\[ m=48,\; T=10\cdot 48^{2}=23040,\; f=\sqrt{\tfrac{23040}{1024\cdot 572}}\approx 0.198 \;\Rightarrow\; 192\times 96,\; N_{\text{soft}}=4\cdot 2=8,\; N_{\text{patch}}=72 \]

Worked example: the 572×1024 image with k = 3, p = 16, Nmax = 10 gives 96×192 pixels, 8 soft tokens and 72 patches, as in Fig. 2.

Guide

A worked example with the Figure 2 numbers. With a pool of three and patches of 16 pixels, m is 48, and a budget of ten tokens allows 23,040 pixels. The scale factor is about 0.198, which gives 96 by 192 pixels after rounding down, so eight soft tokens from 72 patches. You can reuse this calculation to predict your own image token counts.

§2.3\[ 16\,000\ \tfrac{\text{samples}}{\text{s}}\times 0.040\ \text{s} = 640 \ \text{values per audio chunk} \]

12B audio input: each raw 40 ms chunk is a 640-dimensional vector, projected directly into the LLM embedding space.

Guide

Sixteen thousand samples per second times 40 milliseconds gives 640 samples per chunk. In the encoder-free 12B, each such chunk is a 640-dimensional vector projected straight into the LLM, with no extra position code because audio is already ordered in time. For your pipeline, make sure audio is resampled to 16 kilohertz.

§2.3\[ 48\times 48\times 3 = 6912 \ \text{values per image patch} \;\xrightarrow{\ \text{one matmul, 35M params}\ }\; \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}} \]

12B image input: flattened RGB patch times one weight matrix, plus 2D coordinate position embedding, then LayerNorm.

Guide

A 48 by 48 RGB patch holds 6,912 numbers. In the 12B model a single matrix of about 35 million parameters maps each patch into the LLM embedding space, a 2D coordinate position embedding is added, and a LayerNorm follows. This replaces the 550 million parameter ViT used by the larger models.

§2.6\[ d\times 262\,000 \;\longrightarrow\; d\times 4096 \]

E2B/E4B drafters replace the full-vocabulary output projection with a top-k over token clusters, with a similar acceptance rate.

Guide

The drafter's final projection normally scores all 262 thousand vocabulary entries. For E2B and E4B it is replaced by a top-k selection over clusters of tokens, so the matrix shrinks from d by 262,000 to d by 4,096, where d is the drafter's width. The paper reports a similar acceptance rate, so drafting gets cheaper without losing accepted tokens.

The two Vision Transformer sizes: the 550 million parameter encoder has width 1152 and 27 layers, and the 150 million one used by E2B and E4B has width 768 and 16 layers. Both use 16 pixel patches. The smaller encoder is the one you will meet on a free GPU.

Guide

The chat format of the instruction-tuned models. Each turn starts with a turn token and a role, and ends with the end-of-turn token. A think token in the system turn switches on the reasoning trace, and tools use their own tags. For fine-tuning, format every training example this way and end targets with the end-of-turn token.

§8Putting it into practice

Gemma 4 → your project (text + image + voice, QLoRA on free GPUs)

  • Inputs. E2B and E4B take text, images and audio natively (150M ViT + 305M audio encoder), so no speech-to-text pipeline is needed. The 12B also takes audio, but without an encoder. 26B-A4B and 31B have no audio encoder (Table 1): with those you would add an ASR model (for example Whisper) in front. None of the models outputs speech, and the report does not describe video input.
  • Fits a free T4? E2B is the smallest: 2.3B effective, about 5B stored, 4.6 GB for bf16 text weights (Table 3). Loaded in 4-bit for QLoRA it should fit a 16 GB T4 comfortably, and E4B (9.0 GB bf16) plausibly fits too, but check it: image and audio tokens lengthen the sequence and raise activation memory. The T4 has no bf16, and the report notes a per-block scale added so inference is stable in fp16. Still, watch for NaNs.
  • Where to put LoRA. The paper keeps the vision and audio encoders frozen, so do the same. Put LoRA adapters on the decoder's attention and MLP projections, and leave the per-layer embeddings and the MTP drafter alone (the drafter is only for faster decoding). Use the IT chat format of Table 11 and end each target with <turn|> (base PT models end with <eos>), because the paper says fine-tuning needs the right end token.
  • Task the paper points to. Its strongest small-model evidence is on documents (InfographicVQA, OmniDocBench) and speech (FLEURS ASR, CoVoST translation). A spoken question about a document or chart image uses all three inputs. The image budget Nmax is a real trade-off: 280 tokens saves memory, but E2B's InfographicVQA drops from 63.9 to 44.6 (Tables 6 and 12).
  • Fairness and normalization angle. Arabic is the weakest FLEURS language for E4B (WER 0.162 vs 0.065 for English), and it got worse than Gemma 3n (0.101). Arabic vs English speakers is therefore a well-motivated group split for your fairness test. For normalization, the tokenizer splits digits and keeps whitespace, and WER is sensitive to diacritics, punctuation and number format, so normalize the references and outputs the same way before scoring.
Guide

Use E2B or E4B so voice, image and text are all native, and add an ASR model only if you pick 26B or 31B. Load in four bits, put LoRA on the decoder's attention and MLP layers, keep the encoders frozen, and format data with the chat template. A spoken question about a document image matches what the paper tests, and Arabic versus English speech gives a clear fairness split.
